speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make
a reply to a question put yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) concerning ihe proposed salary increases for the civil service. The hon. member remarked that it had been represented that a number of civil servants in certain classes would not get the benefit of the $120 increase, and he asked if the government would reconsider the revision so that these grades would get consideration.
Perhaps we can go more fully into that matter when the supplementary estimates covering these increases are before the House. I might say, however, that the principle underlying these increases is that every member of the service, outside and inside, should get an increase of $120, but exceptions have been made regarding those civil servants who have already partially or fully received that amount of increase since 1924.

In connection with the minister's statement, I have before me a telegram and a letter from the Amalgamated Civil Servants protesting against the exception of the classes referred to in paragraph (d) in the minister's statement the other day, which provides for an increase of only $5 a month for the majority of those civil servants. I would ask, first, if the Secretary of State will tell the House what proportion of the civil servants come within that exception (d). The Amalgamated Civil Servants also draw attention to the increase provided for the railway mail clerks. A comparison is quoted which shows
the railway mail clerk as in receipt of a salary of $1,740, with a minimum of $1,080, as compared with the same class in the United States, who receive a maximum of $2,600 and a minimum of $1,800. I mention this comparison because in other classes the comparison between Canada and the United States is equal. For instance, the district superintendents in both countries receive $4,200, the chief clerks receive $3,600, and there is a very great disparity in the lower grades.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The two questions verge on the same subject. The exception (d) in the report as presented to the House the other night, which I have not before me, covers mostly and almost exclusively, I think, the postal clerks and railway mail clerks. These clerks, Mr. Speaker, demanded an increase in 1924, of $240. They have already received since that time $180 increase, and that is the reason why it is proposed this year to grant only the difference-that is to say $60-meeting, as we understand, fully their demands. Representations have been made to me since the time I made my statement to the House, and we are looking into the matter now. In reference to the question of bringing their salaries up to a parity with the salaries in the United States, we will consider that later on, when the full receipts of the service are on a parity with the receipts of the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister tell me whether the proposed increase includes letter-carriers? I have had a number of inquiries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

Are the rural mail carriers included in that?

speechtext: It all depends whether they come under the Civil Service Commission or not. If they are under contract, of course they would not come under it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
At this late hour of the session, Mr. Speaker, and at this late stage in the debate I do not
1884	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion
intend to take up very much time. I shall endeavour to confine my remarks within the space we are allotting next year to speakers in the House of Commons. Before commencing my remarks dealing with this question, I desire to express my very great regret, which I know is shared by the whole House, that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), on account of illness, is unable to take his place to-day and resume the debate, as was his intention. The hon. member for West Calgary deals with such questions so brilliantly and ably that his speeches, even when hon. members on the other side do not agree with his view, are always listened to with great interest and attention; so that it is really the loss to the House if the hon. member is not able to come here at some time and take part in the debate on a question which he is so pre-eminently qualified to discuss.
The fact that a large proportion of those who have spoken on this question are constitutional lawyers, and that I am not, may possibly bring to this debate something from me that represents the viewpoint of the layman rather than the viewpoint of the constitutional lawyer. We have heard some very able disquisitions upon the question from the standpoint of constitutional law. I intend in my brief remarks to deal with the matter from the standpoint of the man on the street, rather than from the viewpoint of legality. There is no more fascinating study probably in the whole range of politics, at least for a Canadian, than the study of the gradual constitutional development of the British Empire, and many citizens of Canada, in fact perhaps all reading citizens of Canada, have given a great deal of attention and thought to that question. When one remembers that the British Empire comprises a quarter of the people, and a quarter of the area of the globe, that it takes in all races, creeds and nationalities, that it touches all the continents of the world, and that it comprises practically all the various forms of government from the most democratic constitutional monarchy to the government which is perhaps undemocratic because of the backwardness of the people governed, it is easily understood why the question is so interesting.
Never before in the history of the world have we had an empire such as the British Empire. The Roman Empire, the Turkish Empire, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, and any of the empires which have existed in the past have borne only a slight resemblance to the British Empire as it is to-day, and that is why the hon. member for
[Mr. Manion.1
Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), when he was speaking, mentioned that the word "empire" as he understood it, and the word "commonwealth" as he understood it, were not properly applied as they are applied to-day to the British Empire and the British commonwealth of nations. I admit that from the dictionary standpoint if you will, the words "empire" and "commonwealth" do not apply as they are used to-day, but it simply means that the words "empire'' and "commonwealth" are given a broader meaning and a wider significance than they have received in the past, and I believe they are, like many new words which are getting into the dictionary from time to time, and will be interpreted in the future as properly used when used as they are at present. It is apparent to the most superficial reader that the constitution of Canada has been growing as the years go by, just as the British constitution has been growing in the same way. In fact I think it is apparent even to superficial readers that the actual growth has been faster than the legal growth; in other words, that there are clauses in the British North America Act which apparently are still in force, but which are really obsolete, so far as we are concerned. The spirit of the constitution and the letter of the constitution are not exactly the same. There has been an actual evolution towards complete autonomy which has not been recorded at all times in the British North America Act. One author expresses it in this way: that changes have been taking place in inter-imperial relations without resort to imperial legislation, simply by the creating of new conventions of the constitution; and it seems to me that since we may change our constitution without recording such change in the British North America Act, or since the British may change their constitution by new conventions, there is danger of a report of an Imperial conference such as this being accepted by the House without such an amendment as has been moved by my hon. leader. If we accept the report of this Imperial conference without discussion and without making it clear that it is not a legal, binding document upon this House, some day we are likely to find that one of the conventions-and I use the term rather broadly -mentioned in the report may have upon some of the parties to the compact an effect which it was not the intention of this House or of the parties to the compact to permit to happen. I think it was Sir Robert Borden who used the phrase "legal power" as opposed to "constitutional right." For example some of the speakers mentioned the power of

Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion
disallowance by the British parliament of some Canadian legislation, a power which still technically exists, but which has not been exercised for about half a century, and which for that reason is obsolete. Therefore the constitutional right to-day would not permit the British parliament to change or veto our legislation, but the legal power is still existent in the constitutional act.
The same thing is true in regard to the constitution of Great Britain. The king is empowered to veto legislation passed in Great Britain but his practice of doing so is virtually obsolete. In other words, we are gradually becoming a completely autonomous state.
I may be quarrelled with for making that statement, but I shall deal with it in a moment. We are part of an alliance of nation states acknowledging a common allegiance to the crown. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) used the term " unity and liberty ". The term " unity with liberty " appeals to me as better expressing what is meant. Just as England has been becoming more democratic by the king having less power and the people gaining more power, so in exactly the same way we have been growing in the attributes of nationhood. There has been in our constitutional power a gradual growth which, I think, has been satisfactory to most people except some constitutional experts, in some 'cases self-constituted constitutional experts, and perhaps some youthful Canadians who with all the impulse of youth are going ahead as Rosebery one time said, "with all the heedless rhetoric of ambitious youth." Therefore I believe, generally speaking, the gradual evolution of our constitution has been satisfactory to most of the people of this country.
There are a few facts which, it seems to me, as Canadians, whether Liberals, (Conservatives, Progressives or whatever group we belong to, we might as well admit:
1.	That our autonomy has been increasing and is to-day almost complete.
2.	That our international standing among the nations of the world has also been reaching a high position and has to-day almost arrived at the stage of our being a nation absolutely and completely in the eyes of other nations.
3.	That there are to-day in, Canada no colonials. Every one of us is in a sense a national, if I may modify the use of that word a little. We are all nationals in this that we believe our country is developing gradually into a great nation, becoming more and more a powerful nation among the nations of the world. I do not believe any
one takes the reactionary attitude that we should go back on that progress.
4.	That everybody in our country has a strong desire for peace not only at home but internationally. In that regard I think the British commonwealth of nations is a league of nations in itself, helping us very materially towards maintaining the peace of the world. Our own league of nations, the British commonwealth of nations, is actually an example for the larger and more important, if you will, League of Nations which exists and which is not carrying out its functions to the same extent that the British commonwealth of nations is carrying out its functions.
With those general remarks from the Standpoint, as I stated, of a layman, I wish for a few moments to deal with the Imperial conference as it appears to me. As I read in the press the reports of that Imperial conference when they were first published, before we had the authoritative report placed on the table of the House, it struck me that few if any changes were made in our constitutional position. It seemed to be merely a report of things as they were, an announcement in plain English of our position. The London Times called it " an authentic picture of the empire as it is," and it struck me at that time at least that that was a complete description of the result of the Imperial conference.
But since then contradictory statements have been made by various leaders, particularly by some of the prime ministers who attended that conference, and those statements make all those interested in the question of the development of Canada look into the matter a little more deeply. Mr. Bruce, in his speech at Montreal, said there was no modification of status at all. Mr. Hertzog said that the empire signifies nothing more than a mere name. That is a much more extreme statement than that of Mr. Bruce, and our own Prime Minister, if I may boil down his words somewhat, said that this was among the great charters which have stood for a larger freedom.

I desire a little later to say a word about the reference to this being a charter of freedom. All speakers on the other side have not quoted my words in that connection. I prefaced what I said by the words, "in that particular"-and I will refer to it a little later-the particular being that there was nothing new in the report of the conference, but that it rather stated something that had already been stated and acknowledged as a fact. In that particular I compared it to the great charters of history.

Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I certainly do not wish
to do my rigjht hon. friend any injustice in the matter. I believe he made the same objection when the leader of my party was speaking. If one looks at the three assertions, the most one can say is that our Prime Minister's assertion, if we take his words as stated now, agrees more or less with the statement of Mr. Bruce, but neither of them agrees with the statement of Mr. Hertzog of South Africa. Therefore the argument remains the same, that we have good ground for looking into the real reason for some of those statements. The clause that has been most discussed in the report appears on page 12 of the Summary of Proceedings. I will read only the lines in italics. Speaking of the group of self-governing communities, the report states:
They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
With ninety per cent of that probably nobody could quarrel at all; but with the statement that we are absolutely autonomous, absolutely equal one with another, I think, in view of the fact that there is in England the power to change their constitution without submitting the question to any other part of the empire, and that that power does not exist in Canada, we can hardly state truthfully, when looking at the facts that we are absolutely equal constitutionally. The Minister of Justice in his speech stated that there was no inferiority-and I am certainly not arguing for inferiority-as long as we were willing to admit this condition and willing that this condition should continue. I think I am quoting him correctly. Just to admit a condition does not remove it. To admit a fact does not remove it. For example, a man might admit that he was in poverty; he might say that he was perfectly willing to remain in poverty, but that would not make him a millionaire. The same is true in regard to our constitution. To admit that we are willing to continue thus is not necessarily to put us on an equality with Great Britain in this respect. Therefore to my mind it might be well for us to look at the facts without, in doing so, being accused of colonialism or a desire to be subordinate to some other part of the empire.
The claim that has been made by some, that we are in a position of new superiority does not appear to me to be sustained by the facts, for the simple reason that our present status is the result of a gradual growth

hastened, it is true, very materially by the war. Our position as a virtually autonomous self-governing nation within the empire was long ago conceded. One might go back quite far among the records of progress in the empire to prove this assertion, but three or four brief quotations will I think suffice to illustrate the point I am making. For example, in 1911 at the Imperial conference Mr. Asquith is reported as having said that the responsibility for foreign relations could not be shared by the dominions with the British parliament.. In 1912, however, the same Mr. Asquith delivered a speech in which he practically retraced his steps in this regard1 and admitted that there had been an increase fn power on the part of the self-governing sections of the empire; and he recognized their right, later on, of participating in the guidance of foreign affairs in the empire. This shows the growth that was taking place. Richard Je'bb, a much quoted authority who has written many interesting books on this subject, in one of his books published in the year 1911 advocated an imperial parliament or federation; and in the 1911 conference Sir Joseph Ward of New Zealand embodied this proposal in a motion which failed to receive the support of Sir Wilfrid Laurier or any of the other dominion representatives attending t/hat gathering. Since that time the imperial federation idea has I believe become defunct. The same Richard Jebb two years later, in 1913, wrote a book-I cannot at the moment recall the title but I have read it-in which he described the dominions as nation states, and from the idea of nation stales he proceeded to the broader conception of what he called a Britannic alliance. At the Imperial War conference of 1917 our position was clearly stated, and perhaps I may be allowed to quote two or three sentences from the declaration then made:
The Imperial War conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the empire is too important and intricate a subject to be dealt with during the war, and that it should form the subject of a special imperial conference to be summoned as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities.
They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such readjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations of an imperial commonwealth and of India as an important portion of the same.
That was a clear enough definition of our position as seen by the Imperial War conference of 1917. I shall give one other quotation, and that from Mr. Lloyd George.

Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion
It has been cited before in debates on this question, but it will bear repetition. The statement to which I refer was made in 1921 at the Imperial conference, I think, when, speaking of the self-governing parts of the empire, Mr. Lloyd George said:
They are signatories to the treaty of Versailles and of all other treaties of peace. They are members of the Assembly of the League of Nations and their representatives have already attended meetings of the league. In other words, they have achieved full national status and they now stand beside the United Kingdom as equal partners in the dignities and responsibilities of the British commonwealth.
These quotations are, I thiuk, sufficient to show the point of view generally taken in regard to this question. Apparently, therefore, there has been no change in our status as it was recognized some years ago. It has long since been admitted that we were, ultimately at any rate, to be fully autonomous states, and while many other opinions might be quoted to illustrate the widespread acceptance of that fact years ago, it will be admitted, I fancy, that within the past few years, particularly since the war, we have broadened our autonomy. It seems to me that we have developed, from the standpoint of national autonomy to national manhood, just as unconsciously in a way to ourselves, and in a sense as unobserved by other nations, as sons grow to manhood unconsciously to their parents and very often unnoticed by friends and neighbours.
If I may briefly sum up what I have said I shall have concluded that branch of my remarks. We are to-day, in my opinion, virtually independent states within the British Empire, owing a common allegiance to the crown, but not equal to Great Britain so far as the power of making constitutional changes is concerned. There are still many anomalies in our constitution, which anomalies, like others that have existed in the past, will gradually be removed. The Canadian people will without doubt ultimately rule the destiny of this country through its parliament, and if Canadians through their parliament should ever decide to sever the ties of empire and become an independent nation there would be no question about the British parliament accepting that decision. Internationally we are rapidly attaining complete nationhood, as evidenced by our presence at the negotiation of the treaty of Versailles and our signature to the covenant of the League of Nations. And why should we not attain that nationhood when we consider such countries as Bulgaria, Poland, Belgium, the Argentine or Brazil?

Now I wish to deal for a few moments with the remarks of my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa).

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I am going to discuss
briefly now some of the remarks of my hon. friend from Labelle. I regret very much the attitude which that hon. gentleman so often assumes in this House and which, if it does not reflect his true state of mind on the subject, is a serious injustice to himself. At any rate he appears to entertain a strong dislike, if not an absolute hatred, for Britain. It seems to me that such an attitude can do nothing but injure the hon. gentleman's own compatriots by inspiring antagonisms, dissensions, unrest and misunderstandings between them and the other people of this Dominion. Nay, more:	he inspires antagonisms between the people of this country and those of other parts of the empire. This is well demonstrated by his reference to Lord Cave, whom he cited the other day as having expressed an opinion which would certainly be unworthy of a great judge-an opinion alleged to have been offered on a subject which was sub judice in the Privy Council. The hon. member declared that Lord Cave had made the statement while in Canada. Lord Cave has since then, however, absolutely denied the allegation. But suppose that he had made the statement ascribed to him: that would not prove the uselessness of the Privy
1888	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion
Council; it would merely prove the indiscretion of Lord Cave. I have no desire whatever to do the hon. member for Labelle any injustice; my sole intention is to bring about a better understanding among the people of this country and between us and the rest of the empire. I ask, what good can it possibly do for anyone here to be continually taking an attitude which must necessarily result in misunderstanding, not only among Canadians themselves but among the different peoples of the empire?
I may observe-I hope without any suggestion of conceit-that a good deal of my reading has been historical; and let me add that, being so far as I know of pure Irish descent, I am not inclined to give any blind allegiance to England. In other words I am not a blind worshipper at the shrine of England, and I say that quite frankly in view of the remarks I am going to make. Even taking that into consideration, after having read a good deal of history and after having considered world conditions I feel that the world owes a great debt of gratitude to Great Britain for her achievements in parliamentary progress, her advancement in democracy, for her successful colonization of the far comers of the world, and for her general high ideals of liberty and freedom. To make the statement that England has made mistakes, some of which the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou'rassa) continually quotes, is merely to admit that the governments of England have been made up of human beings. Every government .the world has ever seen has made mistakes, even the government of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and looking back at some of the mistakes made by Great Britain it seems to me that she has paid dearly for many of them. I have read a great deal of the history of Ireland, and I say here without caring much' whether it pleases or displeases anyone that I have felt for many years that England made terrible mistakes in her government of Ireland. But she has suffered very much for many of those mistakes, because in the last war, for example, if she had accepted the suggestion made by Mr. Gladstone in the eighties that Ireland should be given the home rule which she possesses to-day, Ireland would have been a very patriotic ally instead of more or less of a thorn in the side of England. Again in the case of the American colonies mistakes were made by a stubborn king and a stupid prime minister which drove those colonies out of the empire; if those mistakes had not been made the United States might have still remained a part of the empire. I submit, however, that taking

into consideration all those mistakes having to do with Ireland, with the American colonies, and with other parts of the world, and putting on the opposite side of the balance the honourable and noble achievements of Great Britain in the advancement of the world, she deserves the gratitude of the whole world for the progress she has helped bring about.
To say that Great Britain has made mistakes may be easily balanced by taking into account some of the mistakes made by other countries, and as I thought of the remarks I am now making I jotted down from memory a few mistakes which came to my mind. Think of the mistakes Spain made in Cuba, for example, which led to the Spanish-Ameri-can war; then the Spanish persecution of the Netherlands. Consider also Austria's oppression of northern Italy in the years gone by; Germany's treatment of the people of Alsace after the Franco-Prussian war; Russia's treatment of Poland and the Tzarism which followed, and the Sovietism which followed the Tzarism and which to my mind is an even worse type of government. Then there was the treatment of the Huguenots by France, and the attempts of Louis XIV and later of Napoleon I to dominate the world and to become despotic rulers of the whole of Europe. I mention these mistakes not to criticize these various countries but to show that other countries have made just as grievous and even greater mistakes than those made by Great Britain.

speechtext:
Yes, probably even in
China, but I will not go into the Chinese situation just now; I will leave that for my hon. friend. Now I will point out one of the good things done by England which should appeal to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and which I am sure does appeal to all members from Quebec sitting opposite. England conquered Canada and took it from France; in the ordinary course of events, especially in the spirit of those days, it was to be expected that England would wipe out the French language entirely to make this a British, English-speaking, dominion. Instead of that there could not be fairer treatment, it seems to me, given to any group of people than was given by Great Britain to the 60,000 French-Canadians who were then living in the province of Quebec. I think her treatment of those French-Canadians at that time is well epitomized in the words of Lord Elgin to Earl Grey in 1848. It is true that Lord Durham did suggest in his report that

Imperial Conference-Mr. Manion
the French language would 'be and perhaps should be submerged, but the words of Lord Elgin are, I think, worthy of being placed on Hansard although they have doubtless been quoted many times before. In 1848 he wrote as follows:
I am very anxious to hear that you have taken steps for a repeal of so much of the Act of Union as imposes restrictions on the use of the French language. ... I must moreover confess that I for one am deeply convinced of the impolicy of all such attempts to denationalize the French. Generally speaking they produce the opposite effect from that intended, causing the flame of national prejudice and animosity to burn more fiercely. subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I do not think any dominion can be kept in the empire by force. I may not have a very keen mentality but I have sense enough to realize that. The situation before this declaration was made was different from that which exists to-day. Speaking for Canada this declaration means nothing at all; it does not add to any liberties or freedom that we had because, starting from the time of confederation, the most responsible statesmen we had declared the position of Canada to be practically what this conference says it is. Therefore our freedom has not been extended.
But there is a marked difference between having an unwritten recognition of our rights, our status and our freedom, and having a written declaration. Prior to this time Canada has not suffered in its liberties. Every person in this country knew that the British parliament would at any time have said to this Canada: If you want to .join the United States, there will be no compulsion from this side of the water to prevent you. This coun-32649-1204
try has been free at any time it chose to go into annexation with the United States republic. Yet that was not declared. Now it is declared, this declaration puts us into a position where we can say to Great Britain: Well, we are going to change our political status; we are going to join with the United States instead of remaining with the motherland. I want if I can to emphasize the point that this country, before this declaration was made, was in a much better position as a part of the empire to remain a part of the empire, and that this declaration does not add anything to our freedom.
I am one of those who believe that Canada has been not only free but under no compulsion ever since confederation to do anything the British government wanted or would try to compel us to do. We have been fairly well a dutiful daughter of the empire, and that is the relationship which I think ought to persist practically as long as we last. These definitions of our status serve materially to encourage all those who believe in Canadian independence, all those who would like to cut the bond that binds us to the mother country. I would be mistaken if they did not become more active now than they have been in the past. We have had a good deal of propaganda in that direction, but it has not met with much success. The people of Canada are too firmly convinced of the wisdom of continuing under present condition* rather than of becoming an independent nation, but this declaration enables us to do anything we like at any time.
There has been some talk about the amendment of the British North America Act. This declaration of status puts this parliament into the position of changing the British North America Act at any time and in any way it chooses. My right hon. friend says that the British North America Act stands where it always stood. That is not the case. Any parliament in the future, ten, twenty, thirty or forty years hence, has only to bring that declaration into this House to enable it to change the British North America Act, or to change any other act, or to pass any law which the majority of this parliament representing the people of Canada desires to pass. It must 'be remembered that the report states that the dominions are:
In no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs.
If that be the case and if that view be taken by some parliament in the future, we can amend our present constitution in any way at all. There can be no escape from that.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. S. RENE MORIN (St, Hyacinthe-Rouville) :
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
However much we may differ regarding the resolution now before the House we can all agree, I think, with the noble sentiments expressed so eloquently by Victor Hugo.
The question of the relations of the various parts of the British Empire inter se and of the relations of each part to foreign countries was the main question considered at the last Imperial conference. It is one of great importance as it involves the destinies of the whole of the empire, and is delicate to deal with because, in the study of this problem, we find no enlightenment in precedents. History has never known such relations and we are handicapped by the rules of international law which have not provided for such conditions.
It is not my intention to study in detail the terms and bearings of each part of the resolutions which were adopted at this conference, I will confine my remarks to a few general ideas on the matter, which in my mind must have been some of the guiding principles of our representatives at this conference and should form the basis of any future developments. The problem which our representatives had to face was to conciliate conditions apparently contradictory, the condition of peoples enjoying their full freedom, claiming full sovereignty and desirous of becoming international persons in the family of nations, with an association or union of a group of sister countries under one nominal head, carrying with it certain restrictions to the rights and liberties of its members.
The evolution of Canada from a crown colony to her present international position has been slow but gradual, steady and inevitable. There were apparently only three solutions to the problem of her relations with the mother country, that is, subordination, federation, or separation.
Subordination was possible for a time, but it could not last. Canadians of English descent who immigrated into Canada were not subject to any degradation; they preserved absolute equality of citizenship with those of their compatriots who had remained on the shores of the mother land; they could not submit for long to a status of inferiority and as their political and economic needs increased they were bound to claim the right to settle them by themselves and in the light of their own interests. As the sense of devotion to the country of their choice or the country of their birth developed in themselves, they were bound to throw off all bonds of inferiority or subordination.
French Canadians who had elected to remain m the land where they were bom and which they loved had perforce to submit for some time to domination, but they were also bound to claim for themselves the right to solve their own problems; government by Downing Street. or by its officials was even more unbearable to them than it was to their compatriots of British origin because it was a foreign yoke.
The troubles and difficulties to which a government by domination gave rise in Canada led certain British statesmen to consider Canada as a millstone around their necks, to lose interest in her welfare and development and to grant her responsible government, avowedly as a first step to separation and independence. It was shortly after this period that a policy of imperial federation began to be preached by certain British statesmen, and the idea took root in the minds of many people in both Great Britain and Canada. The idea of an imperial federation evoked the formation of a political union between a group of countries dispersed throughout the different parts of the world,
1898	COMMONS
Imp. Conference-Mr. Morin (St. Hyacinthe)
rich in natural resources and raw materials susceptible of enormous development, and which, closely and indissolubly united, would take a somewhat predominant place among the nations of the world.
The dominating influence of such an agglomeration of nations was bound to be, for a long time to come, with Great Britain, and naturally her public men were the most enthusiastic protagonists of this new policy, although it had many adherents in the dominions. To many people patriotism meant devotion to the country of their birth or the country of their ancestors; to them Britain was yet the home country and her wealth, her prestige and her power were looked upon by them as their own, even though they had no participation in her government. Any kind of representation in the government ot this federation would satisfy them. Others, however, felt that in such a federation the dominant role would belong to one of the parties and that the position of the others would be of secondary importance; that by such a federation they might be involved in the turmoil of the quarrels and jealousies of the European states with which Great Britain is geographically and economically so intimately connected; that they might be embroiled in mandates, protectorates, extensions of territories and sometimes conquests in which they would have no particular interest and that, on account of the diversity of needs of the different component parts of this federation, a centralized authority might force us to sacrifices which might be unnecessary and prejudicial, consequences which it was best to avoid in every possible way.
Truly imperial when considered from a British point of view, such a federation when applied to countries so far apart, with interests so different and sometimes so contrary, could only mean subordination, inferiority and sacrifices for the citizens of certain of its component parts, so this project of a federation did not materialize* and there remained the third solution, that of separation.
There is in the mind of every human being a tendency, an aspiration, a natural instinct to enjoy the fullest freedom possible; sovereignty, which applying to states means national freedom, is just as much a natural aspiration as individual freedom. This natural instinct which kept us away from federation was bound to draw us towards separation and independence, but in our case these natural and normal aspirations were tempered or mitigated by many factors; ties of blood, ties of affection, common idealistic traditions and a common outlook on public affairs, which TMr. L. S. Morin.]
called for the maintenance of a solidarity inconsistent with separation. The attainment of manhood renders tutelage odious but doea not release the bonds which unite a family together; so attainment of nationhood calls for the removal of all bonds of inferiority, but does not in any way, when these bonds are taken off graciously, alter the sentiments of affection and the spirit of cooperation which unite the members of one family together. So Canada, when she attained nationhood, acknowledging her filiation to Great Britain, could not claim her independence nor wish for separation, and none of the dominions were ready to cut off the ties which bound her to the mother country. Each of them naturally aspired to unfettered freedom and liberty but was ready and anxious to maintain with Great Britain bonds of cooperation entailing a large amount of solidarity, provided these bonds be not imposed forcefully but be voluntarily agreed to as between equals and in the common interest.
Subordination, federation and separation have been left out as a solution of the problem of the relations of the different parts of the Britannic commonwealth, and these relations have taken the character of a partnership, or more accurately, since there are no written undertakings, of an entente which, whilst maintaining the full freedom and liberty of its component parts in all matters domestic or foreign which relate to their own particular interests, yet unites them to preserve the integrity, the influence and the prestige of the whole. Under this system the empire has evolved from a single state to a group of states and the advantages of federation, without its dangers, are being made consistent with the fullest national aspirations and the greatest freedom.
In all matters relating to the internal government of the country, the rights and liberties which are the appanage of independent and sovereign nations have been de facto, enjoyed by the self governing dominions for a long time; and within a few years these rights and liberties have been extended to foreign relations. Thus Canada took part in the negotiations of the Peace conference, signed the treaty of Versailles and entered the League of Nations with the standing of a complete sovereign nation. She has negotiated and signed other treaties through her own ministers, has contracted treaties in the name of the king acting on behalf of Canada-as distinct from the king acting on behalf of the empire-she has made treaties respecting the delimitations of her frontiers, she asserted her freedom from the responsibilities assumed

Imp. Conference-Mr. Morin (St. Hyacinthe)
by the British government without her participation; and has enjoyed in one case, and may have the right whenever she chooses to exercise it, her own diplomatic representation; in a word she has acted as a nation with full powers of sovereignty. This is a state of things w'hich should have satisfied the legitimate* desires and ambitions of all liberty loving and patriotic citizens, but there was still lacking a full understanding and acknowledgment by foreign nations. The resolutions adopted at the Imperial conference have given sanction to these rights and have been a notification to foreign nations of this new status and constitutional freedom. Foreign nations had been slow to grasp such a constitutional development, deceived as they were by the theory of the written law, in many ways inconsistent with this situation.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose for recess the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) had asked me whether I thought that the decisions of the Imperial conference as to the status of the dominions would be accepted by foreign nations without the approval of the parliament of Canada or of that of Great Britain. I had answered him that these resolutions having been unanimously approved by the representatives of all the dominions and by the British government, foreign nations could not properly require a more emphatic statement of the situation. But apart from that, I may say that
approval by the parliament of Canada would not give to the decisions of the Imperial conference any more Weight unless they were approved also by the parliament of Great Britain and by the parliaments of the other dominions which took part in this conference over which we have no control.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Just to be clear,
does the hon. gentleman really take the position that the representatives at the Imperial conference could commit this country to a certain line of action without any reference at all to the parliament of Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
We must make a distinction. There were no active obligations undertaken at the conference in the name of Canada. There was merely a declaration of our new status. That is the purport of these resolutions. They do not carry any new obligation that I know of. These resolutions, moreover, have left unsettled a certain number of points which were referred to in the very remarkable speech made by a colleague of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre sitting on this side of the House; they have left unsettled certain conditions which are the last vestiges of our colonial days, and a formal approval of these resolutions by parliament at this stage might give to these conditions a character of finality which is not to be desired.
The views which I was expressing, Sir, were that the resolutions adopted at the Imperial conference had acknowledged that we had the right to exercise practically all the functions of a sovereign state, but that these yet lacked the full sanction and acknowledgment by for-' eign nations, and the importance of these resolutions lies in the fact that they were a notification served upon foreign nations of our new status and constitutional freedom. Foreign nations had been slow to grasp our constitutional development, deceived as they were by the theory of the written law, in many ways inconsistent with such independence, but which under the unwritten constitution of Great Britain is superseded by usage and practice. There was need of a public pronouncement in respect of this new status, and it was the main mission of the last Imperial conference to make it.
There are, and there will be for some time yet, different schools qf thought in the dominions on this matter of the relations between the component parts of the Britannic commonwealth, and it seems an anomaly that these resolutions should have been commended
1900	COMMONS
Imp. Conference-Mr. Morin (it. Hyacinths)
by practically all groups. The inconsistency is more apparent than real, because, as a matter of fact, these resolutions do not fundamentally change our relations with Great Britain or the other parts of the British Empire; they do not create new rights; they definitely sanction rights already exercised and acquired; they raise the international standing of the dominions to a status of equality with that of Great Britain, and they alter accordingly the forms and proceedings of their relations. They cannot be read as meaning in any way a parting of the ways from the commonwealth, but the nature of the ties which unite the dominions to the mother country has lost any character of inferiority or subordination which existed in the past, to take up the character of an association between free countries, entered into voluntarily for their mutual benefit. Such a modification could only respond to the expressed or latent sentiments of all citizens having in their heart a natural and normal aspiration to manhood and to nationhood; it means no disintegration of the empire; on the contrary, if I am not mistaken, it will produce more cohesion. It could not therefore but satisfy all shades of opinions, all of which could find in it some comforting features.
The importance of these resolutions cannot be minimized. Their publication made a tremendous sensation throughout the world as was shown by the commentaries of the foreign press, and there was everywhere a ready disposition to recognize the new international standing of the dominions, and to alter relations accordingly.
One of the keenest students of the British constitution and of things Canadian, Mr. Lawrence A. Lowell, the president of Harvard University, in an article published in the April number of Foreign Affairs expressed the following appreciation of the consequences of these resolutions.
As a result of this conference he says that "the self-governing dominions have become legally and politically, in both domestic and foreign matters, independent states"; they have been brought "to a condition of full constitutional independence." These resolutions are "a notice that the dominions have come of age, have full rights of citizenship among the states of the world, and are to be treated accordingly." But the "spirit of cooperation remains strong," he adds, and as a result of the work of the conference "the cohesion of the different parts of the empire will become stronger rather than weaker."

I concur in these conclusions, Mr. Speaker, and holding these views I can only look upon these resolutions as of momentous importance, as marking an epoch in the history of our country, and commend the work of the Prime Minister and his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) at this gathering.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will probably not be useful to the House for me to make any remarks at this stage of the proceedings in the discussion which has your attention, but I feel that this is one of the most important matters with which we have to deal during the present session. While there is not a report before us for adoption or rejection there are embodied in the discussion ideas which have to do with our very existence as part of the British Empire. I do not hesitate to say that I am of those who feel that we must not in any way, by thought or deed, interrupt in even the slightest measure the continuity of the connection of this Dominion with the British Empire, that we must go on for all time an indissoluble part and parcel of that empire. I look with a great deal of apprehension upon reports such as this which deal with so important a subject, and yet are not considered worthy by those who present them to be the subject of a motion in this House. If, as has been truly said,
I take it, the Prime Minister and his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were merely in conference with representatives of other parts of the empire, without their deliberations or conclusions having any binding force, then the documents we have before us as a report of the Imperial conference could carry no sanction for any action to be taken. That seems to be agreed upon. However, it was brought back as an achievement, as something that our representatives at that conference had been able to get for us. It was represented as being a new charter in fact, and as far away as the Dominion of South Africa we heard from the Prime Minister of that British dominion that it meant the end of the British Empire. When views so divergent concerning the results of this conference have been expressed by our friends in South Africa, our friends in the Irish Free State, and our friends, the constitutionalists, who are so ready to inveigh against the principles of our constitution, we should have something concrete and definite with which this parliament might either agree or disagree. Even to have brought in a report which has no sanction, which does not carry with it the endorsation of parliament, and which is

Imperial Conference-Mr Geary
met without any response, and left on Hansard, or on the records of the House in the terms in which it was brought to us, must, it seems to me, carry some implication in the future. We cannot tell how this matter will be taken up in time to come. It may be argued from this deliverance which has been brought back to us that this may be the case or that may be the case. Who is to say? If it is only a report, the presentation of which elicits no response, and which is denied the endoi'sation of the House, then I say it would have been better never to have been written at all. If it has been placed before us by the Prime Minister and has become a part of the records of the House, then I think the House should declare that it does not agree either with what different people in South Africa have said about it, or what anyone in the future may care to deduce from the words 'of that report. To my mind the amendment of my hon. leader (Mr. Guthrie) suggests the only way of dealing with the subject at the present moment. That is, if there are implications to be drawn from the report, we should deny them and say that this House is not bound by any implication to be drawn from that report. It seems to be sound common sense that we should be on record in some such way as that. Personally I am not afraid of imperialism, either the imperialism which some of my hon friends to my left, who do . not altogether deny that they are of the communist party-

I am glad to have that assurance. That leaves it in a more or less definite form. Be that as it may, there is a certain school of thought, communist or otherwise as you may call it, which distrusts imperialism, 'because imperialism means to them the setting of the workers of one
country against the 'workers of another, and they fear the term "imperialism," because imperialism to them does mean that the common interests of the workers of a country are perhaps interfered with by that sort of imperialism which demands that the material interests of the workers of one country shall involve the interests of the workers of another country. That is the imperialism of my hon. friend. The imperialism objected to by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is that which would involve the Dominion of Canada in war. That is a fetish with him, almost an obsession. He seems to visualize some condition in which the Dominion of Canada is to be drawn into a war. Where the Dominion of Canada has gone into a war, an imperial war if you like to call it such, she has gone into it wholeheartedly, with the assent of the people through their representatives in parliament. I am free to subscribe to this: that if the occasion Should ever arise where the interests of the British Empire are involved, and in which we feel we are interested and should take part, then no one but the representatives of the people here in parliament should say whether or not we should take part in that war. I do not subscribe to any doctrine which says that the people of the country should be called upon to decide it, but the elected representatives in the House of Commons in this country should be able to decide the matter, as they have always done in the interests of Canada. I do not say that every war that occurs in which the empire is concerned necessarily involves Canada, but there may be wars in whidh we have such a vital interest, even if it does not touch our shores, that the people of Canada will rise to say that we must take our share in imperial defence or otherwise as the case may be.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: As citizens of Canada, are we not at war when Britain is at war, no matter whether we go to war ourselves or not?

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right. It is almost a truism that as we are a part of the British Empire when the empire is at war we are at war, and I think nobody will find fault with that declaration. The Dominion of Canada has risen from a small beginning to a mighty place among the nations of the world. It has risen as part of the British Empire. It depends for a great deal of its force and' effect throughout the world upon the fact, not that it is an independent nation or that it has an independent status, not that it can be said to be separated from the British Empire, but, as I said before, because it is always indissolubly a part of the British
1902	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Geary
Empire. If my hon. friend lias any fear that the design of those who advocate continuity of membership in the British Empire, is to look forward to some controversial occurrence, such as a war, he is mistaken. We are not looking for such a thing, or advocating it. There is no such thing as the militarist or jingo spirit existing on this side of you, Sir, but we do feel that we cannot sit as members of this House- and I speak for myself now-and remain content always accepting the position that although we may be bound to take care of our own shores, we are not bound under any circumstances to protect ourselves by land or sea elsewhere on this globe. I am one of those who feel that if the conference report means anything, it means that we have attained to such a position that we are in a sense, not necessarily autonomous, but independent, so that for instance in ease of war we cannot be called upon for contributions by way of taxes or anything of that sort. We are of course autonomous in that sense, but I cannot understand a relationship which disclaims any dependence upon the British Empire, but which is still content, without assuming one cent of the expense, to accept the protection of the British Empire even when our interests are vitally concerned in other parts of the world.
I do not approach this subject in any partisan spirit. That is not my object in saying what I have to say. I feel deeply that such conclusions as have come before us crystallized in the report of the Imperial conference will, unless we are very careful, tend in the direction of the separating, if you like to call it so, in one sense or another of this dominion from the rest of the dominions of the British Empire. That is why I dread to see part of our constitution put into writing. Except in so far as the British North America Act may be considered a written constitution, we have lived not under a written constitution but under a constitution that has grown up from precedent to precedent. It has been satisfactory so far, and for that reason I dread very much seeing put into writing any declaration of our constitutional or any other kind of status, especially when we know perfectly well and have known since the war and long before, that nowhere is there an intention to interfere with us in our external or internal affairs; that England, while she might be very sorry and hear with regret of any determination on the part of this country to sever itself from the empire or from the homeland, would raise neither hand nor voice to deter us from so doing if that was our sincere wish and desire. We have been independent in that sort of way for many long years, and

nothing was required to be put into writing at this stage to declare what we already knew well. That has been one of my objections to this Imperial conference report, that we are reducing to writing something of which we do not know the meaning, something which in the future may be construed for or against this view or that so that no man knows what the result may be.
What is the answer to that? The answer from the other side of the House is that the report does not bind in any way; that it is simply an arrangement reached by those attending the conference; that it does not involve Canada or the House of Commons. If that be the case, why was it done? If it was meant to be a record of attainment to be crystallized into something that the people could look at so as to see what was done, we should have that statement from the government. As it stands now it is on the records of this House without any sanction at all, and the only sensible course this House can bake is to adopt the amendment moved by my hon. leader (Mr. Guthrie) stating definitely that, no matter what the report may say or what inference may be drawn from it, it does not mean certain things as are set out in my hon. friend's amendment.
We are to-day faced with the situation that we have in the empire of China a danger to many of our nationals, how many I do not know. I have heard it stated that there are as many as six thousand. I do not care how many there are, they are just as much entitled to the protection of their lives and property if they be only one hundred as if they be one thousand. We are, as I understand the matter, not taking any steps directly in regard to that situation. If we are independent, if there is an autonomy, a status of sorts that relieves us of obligations to the British Empire and the empire from obligations to us and dissociates us from any responsibility as members of the British Empire, we would be at this time taking some steps to ensure that the lives and property of our nationals in China were protected. There are missionaries, business men and others there, with their wives and children.

I know the hon. member i3 serious in what he says, but I believe his view is mistaken. I do not believe the arts of peace extend that far. From what I have read of proceedings in China, the presence there of United States as well as British gunboats has had a considerable effect thus far at all events in preserving lives and property. Perhaps when the millennium comes, we shall be able to cast aside all means and methods of offence and defence, rest secure in the feeling that every man will treat another as his brother and that nobody will be in trouble the world over. That has not happened as yet anywhere, it certainly has not happened in China. I instance that only as indicating the curious discrepancy between the definition of autonomy and independent status and the actual facts as they exist in China at the present time.
As one who has scanned the report more or less closely I feel there is in it nothing that causes concern at the present moment. I do not think however we should be called upon to adopt it in its entirety without very careful consideration. The government, having through its leader and the Minister of * Justice brought the report before this House,
should be prepared to present it to the House with a definite recommendation, and let it be discussed backwards and forwards, through and through, until we know to where it leads and where it has left us, so that this House may have an opportunity of deciding now on the spot exactly what it is prepared to do in regard to the report. But having the matter before us in this vague way, one cannot get away from it by the mere declaration that it binds nobody, ministers of the crown have subscribed to it one way or another. Therefore the resolution of my leader is along the only lines that this House can safely adopt.
As we go along we find in this country people who are taking advantage of almost every opportunity that offers in some way or another, perhaps only by word, to distinguish between our position and that of the other dominions of the British Empire, to separate us somewhere, to take away the appeal to the Privy Council, to have a king of Canada instead of the king which we have at the present moment, to do this, that and the other, all little matters that go towards a general drift in the way of separatism. I feel that the people of Canada do not desire any such thing.
I believe we have prospered and been happy in our connection with the British Empire, and we can continue to be happy in that connection. We can go forward in the eyes of the world never so well as we can as part and parcel of the British Empire. Anything that tends, even by suggestion or implication, in the slightest way to destroy the ties binding us to the British Empire is abhorrent to me. We should guard against anything of that sort, because I believe the people in this Dominion as represented in this House value as they value nothing else their Canadian nationality and their Canadian nationality as it now is part and parcel of the British Empire. We can go on together as we have done in the past. But strong as that empire may be, let us not by any act or deed of ours, by anything we may say, tend to dislocate the union now existing between us. Let us play our part in conserving the strength of that beneficent empire. In that strength, serene and proud, we in Canada will continue to be part and parcel of the British Empire, never to be dissociated from it, pursuing our own way and proud of our own country, but prouder of it because it is an integral part of a great agency of civilization and advancement which the world has come to regard as its main instrument for progress.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Before touching upon the
amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) I should like to comment on what seems to me to have been a deliberate effort on the part of some hon." gentlemen opposite to misrepresent what I have said with respect to the significance of the recent Imperial conference. My hon. friend from St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) was, I think, the first one to seek to have the House infer that I had made a statement to the effect that the report which was the outcome of the recent Imperial conference was in the nature of a charter which had been wrested from the British government, and that such a statement indicated an attitude of arrogance-I am not quoting the hon. gentleman's words but their meaning and intent-which the people of this country would not wish the leader of the administration to assume. The leader of the opposition, in the course of his remarks, seemed to me to be endeavouring to have that impression gain ground by quoting merely a part of my utterance, and by declining to take notice of the correction I wished to have made, when I drew his attention to the fact that I was being only partially quoted, and sought to have the full statement I had made presented to the House. Instead, he said that my remarks would be found in Hansard exactly in the terms he had quoted, which was not true. There have been other references by other speakers to the same effect, and in view of this fact I think I am justified in asserting that hon. gentlemen opposite have deliberately sought to have a certain impression created with respect to what I had said as to the significance of the conference, which impression my remarks would warrant in no respect.
Perhaps I can put the position in its true light by reading to the House from the speech of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, the interruption on my part and his reply thereto. On March 29, 1927, as recorded in Hansard, the leader of the opposition made the following statement:
I place side by side the statements made by three of the prime ministers who attended the conference of 1926. First, I take the statement made by the Prime Minister of Australia when he was in Canada in January last as reported in the press at the time. He said:
"There is nothing really new in the status or relations of the British dominions as a result of the recent conference. The rights now enjoyed have existed ever since the termination of the war."
That is clear and distinct language which we all understand. Then I compare with that the statement of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister made in this House on December 13 last, when he said:
[Mr. Geary 1
"I believe the work of this conference will take its place in history by the side of those great charters which have stood in one form or another for a larger freedom."
Next I place side by side with that the statement attributed to the Prime Minister of South Africa, who said:
"The British Empire now exists as a name only."
When three of the participants in conference make statements so irreconcilable as those which I have just read, it is little wonder that the public in this country and perhaps in other parts of the British world are at a loss to know what actually did take place.
I interrupted at that stage, as Hansard shows:
Mr. Mackenzie King: I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to mislead the House as to what I said or the significance of it. He has read a part only of what I said. I stated that the resemblance to the charters of a larger freedom lay in the fact that none of them purported to set forth anything that was new, but rather to register the point that had been attained

exactly the same meaning and intent as that conveyed by the reference of the hon. Prime Minister of Australia, which my hon. friend has read.
Mr. Guthrie: No, it is a very different statement, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Mackenzie King: No, it is not.
Mr. Guthrie: The language can mean only one thing, that this larger freedom of which the Prime Minister speaks is a new acquisition to the self-governing powers of this country, or something to this effect.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Would my hon. friend do me the justice of reading the remainder of that statement, and not take one sentence and separate it from its context?
Mr. Guthrie: I will inform my right hon. friend through you, Mr. Speaker, that the statement is to be found in full in Hansard of December 13 last, and that the quotation which I have read is accurate.
Now I would ask the House to refer to Hansard of December 13 last, bearing in mind the words of my hon. friend, that the quotation as he gave it was accurate. I would now point out to the hon. gentleman that the quotation was not accurate, for not only did he not associate the sentence with the paragraph but he did not even quote the entire sentence. He gave part of a sentence, and that part only which would leave a completely misleading inference. The sentence to which I refer in my remarks made on December 13 is as follows:
In that particular, I believe the work of this conference will take its place in history, so far as the statement of inter-imperial relations is concerned, by the side of those great charters which have stood in one form or another for a larger freedom.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition omitted altogether the words, "in that particular," which began the sentence. What *

Imperial Conjerence-Mr. Mackenzie King
was "that particular"? It is indicated in the words immediately preceding:
May I say here what I said publicly in London before coming away, that I believe from the Canadian point of view the merit of the conference will be not in a statement of what has been gained so much as in the statement of what has been attained and is now acknowledged to be altogether beyond debate. I think it is true that all the great charters of freedom in British history have for the most part not purported to introduce anything new or revolutionary. They have purported to be a statement of those rights which the citizens of the day believed were theirs and which they regarded as established. They were a formal statement which could be appealed to by future generations as indicating the point of agreement that had been reached with respect to the several matters with which they dealt.
Then followed my words, "in that particular," and so forth. The leader of the opposition omitted those words, and when I asked him to be good enough to do me the justice of quoting the sentence precisely he declined to do so. He omitted the words "in that particular" but quoted the remainder of the sentence:
I believe the work of this conference will take its place in history, so far as the statement of inter-imperial relations i's concerned, by the side of those great charters which have stood in one form or another for a larger freedom.
There followed then these further words:
I believe this great conference, once party controversy is removed and we get a true perspective of it, will stand out in history as a conference which has revealed how broad, deep and enduring within the British Empire are the foundations of national autonomy and imperial unity.
I submit that anyone reading the full statement as 1 have now given it, will find it impossible to draw from it the inference which hon. gentlemen opposite have been seeking to give to my remarks, not only in this debate but in discussions throughout the country. I should not like to think that my hon. friend had misrepresented me deliberately and I hope he will now admit that I was right in taking exception to his quotation of what I had said as being only partial, and his not giving to my words the full meaning that attaches to them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what was the original statement I made in reference to the significance of the conference. I have read the statement made in this House after returning from the conference. Let me now read the statement I made before leaving England. It was made at a dinner given by the Empire Parliamentary Association at the House of Lords in England on November 27, the concluding day of the conference, which
dinner was attended by representatives from the other dominions as well as by members of the British government, all of whom were called upon to address the gathering. The statement which I made at the time and which in substance I have repeated since will be found in the London Times of the day following the dinner, a copy of which I have in my hand:
For a time, the real work of the conference may be obscured in controversy, but when controversy subsides, and history lends a truer perspective, it will come to be recognized, not only in all parts of the British Empire, but by the world at large that the conference of 1926 has revealed foundations of national autonomy and imperial unity deeper, broader and more enduring than many have dreamed.
Speaking for the Dominion of Canada, I can say that the pride of our people in the achievements of the conference will, as respects Canada's relations in domestic and external affairs, lie not in what has been gained, but rather in what has been attained, and is now- no longer open to debate. Our pride will be the greater in that this acknowledgement is made without a dissenting voice; that in all that has been recorded you of the motherland and we of the dominions are in complete accord. The charter of the liberties we individually and collectively enjoy may, to appearances, have been enlarged. In reality, there has been, as respects British political institutions, natural development along inevitable lines.
That was the statement made in the presence of the British ministers and the representatives of the other dominions. No exception that I could discover was taken by anyone who was present or indeed by the British press, and it was not until this particular statement was misrepresented in the manner I have indicated that exception was naturally taken to what was supposed to have been the claim I made with respect to some great gain which had been made at the Imperial conference at the expense of the British government or of Great Britain.
