speechtext:
Let me read
the statement made by Mr. Baldwin, the Prime Minister of England, on the same occasion, tvhich will be found to be identical in meaning if not in the same terms. I desire to give this for the purpose of making it clear that the criticism which hon. gentlemen opposite are endeavouring to focus on the leader of the government in Canada is applicable in equal measure to the prime ministers of all the self-governing dominions and the Prime Minister of Great Birtain, as well as to the other members of the British government who were present. As long as that is understood I have no objection to my hon. friends levying any criticism they may have to offer, but I do take exception to having the impression go abroad not only throughout the British Empire but throughout the world as well that so far as Canada was concerned her representatives adopted an attitude which was singular in this particular direction, and not comparable to the attitude taken by the prime ministers of the other self-governing dominions. 1 will just quote one paragraph from the remarks made by Mr. Baldwin:
"We emerged from the war transformed. Great Britain emerged no longer isolated. Science had decreed that whether Great Britain liked it or not she was for all time an integral part of Europe. The dominions emerged matured, grown up to man's estate and conscious of their manhood, with its privileges and its obligations. We have recognized that fact," continued Mr. Baldwin, "we have acknowledged it to one another and that is really what we have said in this historical document. We are the last people to indulge in theories and definitions. but we have stated there a fact. We have tried to see things as they are and put them forth for the world to read. That is a very different thing from plucking a plant up by the root every year to see how it is growing. We have never done that and we have never attempted to define terms too closely, even at the risk of being thought an illogical people. Now we have published to the word our conception of the status of the communities which comprise the British Empire.
If my hon. friend will take those words of, the Prime Minister of England and put them beside my own words which I have quoted, he will find that their meaning and significance is to all intents and purposes identical. Mr. Baldwin was expressing appreciation of the fact that the representatives of the dominions and the representatives of the British government were as one in their general concensus of view as to the status existing between the different self-governing parts of the British Empire in their inter-imperial relations. He was expressing further an appreciation which I think was felt generally throughout the British Empire that there had

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
been a consensus of view which was unanimous on that particular matter.
Now, what was the status on which we all agreed? Reference has often been made in the course of the debate to the text of the report itself; we will grasp its significance better if we take broadly the possible alternative conceptions of. the relations of the different self governing parts of the British Empire to one another, Great Britain included. There is no escaping one or other of these alternatives. Either the dominions, in relation to Great Britain, are in a position of colonial subordination, or they are in a position of equality of status. There is no escaping this alternative: in relation to the dominions either the position of Great Britain is one of imperial control, or else it is one of equality of status. Now you cannot get away from one or the other of these positions; and when you come to discuss the questions that arise as between the different parts of the British Empire there comes immediately to the fore, the query, on what fundamental basis are you going to settle these questions? Are you going to lay down the basic principle as one of imperial control on the part of Great Britain and colonial subordination as respects the dominions, or are you going to say that the basis that has been achieved- not all in one year but over a large number of years-the point that has now been reached, that has been attained in the evolution of the great structure of empire, is one where the self-governing dominions hold an equality of status with the mother country? I venture to say that understood in that broad light there is not an hon. member of this House who will take exception to that statement of the position. See what the effect is the moment that position is acknowledged. So long as it is not acknowledged you have within the self-governing dominions the strongest kind of reason for agitation against imperial control, the strongest kind of reason for agitation against colonial subordination. The minute the status is declared and known to be one of equality to permit of effective cooperation between the different parts that moment you remove throughout the empire the basis for agitation on that particular ground. I wish to say that when the conference met there was in one or two parts of the British Empire a great deal of agitation which the British government I know viewed with a good deal of concern. There was a condition very unsettled in South Africa; there was a certain unsettled condition in Ireland. The minute the position was made clear that so far as the relations of Great Britain to these dominions was concerned it was not one of imperial control but was one of equality of status-each self-governing part of the empire in its relation to the other part being on a footing of equality for the purpose of effective cooperation-that minute the agitation subsided and those responsible for it were obliged to change their note.
Take the effect of the conference, for that, after all, is the best way to judge of results. What has been the effect in South Africa? The feeling in South Africa to-day towards Great Britain is vastly different from what it was before the conference took place. It is not one of estrangement from Great Britain. On the contrary there is every evidence of a desire on the part of South Africa to remain within the British Empire and a feeling of pride in the position of South Africa in the empire; and the same, I believe, is true in regard to the Irish Free State. I wish to take very strong exception to the words which were spoken here this morning by my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hock-en) to the effect that there was represented at that conference a couple of nations of the empire that were seeking to separate, and that the representatives of Canada were doing their part in helping to make it easy for them to get away. Those are not the exact words of the hon. gentleman but that is their intent and meaning. I say to my hon. friend that I do not think that he uttered the sentiments of his own heart or his own mind when he used those words; he was talking from a purely political motive at that time. I do not believe that my hon. friend feels in his heart that the representatives of this Dominion went to that Imperial conference with any such object in their minds-

has, those who are closely in touch with the British government in London, if he would enquire from them as to the kind of part which was played by the Minister of Justice and myself at the Imperial conference- whether it was a part which sought to make the problems of empire more difficult, or whether it was a part which to the uttermost sought to help to bring about unity in imperial affairs. If hon members opposite will communicate with those members of the British cabinet who were at that conference, I challenge them to. find one who will do other than admit that the part played by Mr. Lapointe and myself was the part of men who were doing their utmost to bring about unity, and to remove the occasions for discord within the British Empire; and I affirm that it comes with pretty poor grace from gentlemen who profess to have such a love of the empire, and to be the especial exponents of empire, to do their utmost to destroy the work that has been done by the representatives of this country in company with the representatives of other parts of the empire with whom they find no fault and whom they are over zealous to praise.
Now let me go back to the statement I have made as to the results of the conference as embodied in its report being worthy of being placed beside the great charters in Britsh history. I have in my hand a copy of the London Spectator which I think is as Conservative an organ as is published in Britain. Certainly no one will challenge its high standing, no one will challenge its interest in the empire, no one will challenge the great skill with which it is edited. The dinner at the House of Lords 'took place on November 27. On that same day the London Spectator came out with an article on the conference. I had not seen this article at the time I made my speech; I had at the time no knowledge of its existence. What was the view this great British journal took of the significance of the Imperial conference? The article is headed "The British Commonwealth's Charter of Freedom" and the first paragraph reads as follows:
The eagerly awaited report of the Inter-imperial Relations Committee of the Imperial conference was issued on Saturday, November 20, and an epoch-marking document it is, whatever may he said to the contrary. For years to come the report will be regarded as a charter of freedom for the British commonwealth of nations. The document may well rank with our most important state papers, for in it are set forth the basic principles on which the British Empire rests. Never was the genius of the British people for adapting their political institutions to the changing needs of the day more

apparent. Here is no written constitution which will bind future generations, but rather a confession of faith in what the empire stands for in 1926, and an indication of how best to insure its permanence.
Now there is a statement identical in its intent and meaning with the one I made, and to which such exception is being taken at the present time. It does not say that the work of the conference amounted to nothing. It attaches very great significance to the fact that we have reached a point in the evolution of empire where we were able by common accord definitely to state a position of vast consequence to all parts of the empire.
But let me quote from a speech made by the Bight Hon. Mr. Amery, Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, a speech delivered at the Constitutional Club on December 16th, and reported in the London Daily Times of December 17th. The speech was on the Imperial conference and it is easy to see what significance Mr. Amery gives to the conference, speaking on behalf of the British government. This is the quotation from the Times:
The conference had cleared the way for future cooperation by getting rid of certain misunderstandings as to the relative position of the dominions and ourselves which had survived into recent years and were a cause, not only of difficulty as between the dominions and ourselves in our efforts to cooperate, but also of internal political difficulty in more than one dominion. Lord Balfour had achieved not the least of his many great achievements in being responsible for a report which marked a new and useful stage in empire cooperation. It might be said with truth that there was really nothing new in the conclusions of the Balfour committee, but this report was only typical of many other great documents in our constitutional history. Our procedure has never been to lay down a constitution for the future, but rather, from time to time, to see how the constitution had developed and to take note of the stage which had been reached. That was, in essence, what the Balfour report did.
Exactly the same statement in intent and meaning as the one which I have made as to the significance of the conference itself.
Now I come to the next point that has been stressed in this debate, and that is the criticism of myself and the government for not submitting the conference report for the approval of parliament. My hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence^St. George (Mr. Cahan) gave, I think, three grounds on which he felt the report should have been submitted: First, that I had stated when speaking in the debate on the Address last December that it was the intention of the government to submit the report to the House; second, that the report of 1923 had been submitted in whole or in part for the approval

of parliament, and therefore that this report should also be submitted to parliament; and thirdly, that I had no right to speak on behalf of the people of Canada, that the only body that had that right was this parliament, and that I should put the report before parliament so that parliament could pronounce upon it.
I think I have stated correctly in intent and meaning my hon. friend's different arguments.
I did state, Mr. S'peaker, in December last that it was the intention of the government to submit the report- to parliament for its approval. But sometimes second thoughts are better than first thoughts. I confess that 1 had no sooner made that statement to parliament than I was told that my reason for so doing was to force a division in this House: that I knew I had come back from the conference with a report that would command the confidence of parliament and would help to give the government a good majority, and that I was intending to put this report before parliament and compel a division upon it, or else the acceptance of the report in its entirety without division, which would,, of course, bring greater -credit to the administration than ever.

In Great Britain in the House of Commons, as far as I can discover, they have not even debated the question of the conference. Questions have been asked of the ministers and the min-

The part in regard to

Let me explain to the House why a particular part was submitted to parliament, and in so doing I suggest that it forms a kind of precedent which we might well follow in regard to matters contained in the reports of Imperial conferences. There were two reports of the conference of 1923, one the report of the Imperial conference and the other of the Imperial Economic conference, dealing with the same class of subject matters as are dealt with in the one report of the last conference. Those two reports were placed before parliament just exactly as this report was placed by tabling, and by order of the House having copies printed and distributed. That was done in 1924. The conference was held in 1923. In the session following no action was taken on the report. It was not submitted for approval. In the session of 1925 no action was taken, and in 1926 the part of the report which related to a certain procedure with respect to treaties was presented to parliament and parliament was asked to adopt it. Why? Because in the interval there had been received from the British government a statement of some of the matters that would be on the agenda of the ensuing conference, and one was the further consideration of the question of treaties, the procedure, with respect to negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties. This parliament has taken a different view than some of the other parliaments of the empire with respect to the approval of treaties. We have taken the position that a treaty cannot be held to be binding on Canada until it has been approved by our parliament-that it cannot be ratified until approved by parliament. Now there had been no expresion of view from the Canadian parliament on that all-important matter, and it was to get an expression of view on that important matter, to get the en-dorsation of this House on the course of procedure laid down and which we had already followed with respect to three or four treaties which we had negotiated that this House was asked to approve that particular part of the report before the conference of 1926 took place. So that when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and myself went to the con-

In the course of my remarks the other day, I mentioned that there was one particular thing, one single act out of all the rest, in regard to which the Minister of Justice and myself, acting on behalf of the government of Canada, felt that we were justified in committing this country to some extent, in the belief that in so doing we would have the full support of parliament.
In the discussion at the conference on the question of commercial air routes relating to an immediate probable development of airship navigation, a request was made by the Minister of Air to the governments assembled at the conference for one or more to agree to cooperate with the British government in making a test of aerial navigation for commercial purposes, by going the length of agreeing to undertake to put up a mooring mast to which airships could be moored and to gather meteorological data sufficient to enable those who were doing the navigating to feel secure in the course which they were taking. That request was made in an informal way; there was no resolution or anything of the kind about it. I said to my colleague who was beside me: it seems to me that the people of Canada will welcome an experiment which is going to help to develop trade between England and our dominion, no matter how that development takes place. We all know we are on the eve of great developments in

air flights, and at the conference the Minister of Justice and I knew that Africa, Australia and India had already established their commercial routes with flights from one part to the other. We felt that we would be derelict in our duty if we did not take advantage of that moment to endeavour to get the first flight of airships across the ocean between Canada and Great Britain rather than between Australia, or Africa, or some other part of the empire and Great Britain. So we said that we would be prepared, when parliament met, to ask parliament to vote what was necessary to pay for a mooring mast and to undertake that particular work of experimentation. That item is in the estimates and it will come before parliament, in fact the estimates are before the House now. If we have taken a wrong stand in that, parliament can review our stand; parliament can refuse to ipass that estimate.
We were not endeavouring to escape the authority of parliament; but ministers of the crown from the nature of their position are obliged to act or to fail to act on particular occasions, and they can be held as liable for the one course of procedure as for the other. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that I had no right to speak for Canada; they declare that I should not have dared to say whether we were at one with other parts of the empire. Yes, and the man who has just said "hear, hear" is responsible for much of the language of that kind. Let me say that nothing could be more unpatriotic, more unworthy of a British citizen than such an insinuation. I tell hon. gentlemen that there is no man within the empire who has a greater love for it than I have; there is no man who believes more strongly than myself in the wisdom of preserving the empire as the greatest agency for peace and goodwill and progress in the world. It is for that reason that I say now, emphatically, that when a party or its members seek to have it appear to the world at large that one who is imbued with that spirit, and who entertains that regard for the British commonwealth of nations is engaged in an endeavour to dismember the empire, they are going a long way towards sowing seeds which some day may bear the kind of tares they would not wish to see. It is easy enough to sow the wind but the time comes thereafter when you reap the whirlwind, and I tell my hon. friends opposite that any man who seeks to make party gain out of imperial questions fails to play his part as a true British citizen or a patriot. I do not think I need repeat that when I left Canada I made it clear that so far as our Dominion was concerned our relations with the mother country, as well as with other parts of the empire, eojild not be better
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
than they were. From the moment I entered upon the proceedings of the conference until the very close of those proceedings every effort I could possibly put forward was made with the sole object of seeking, as far as I could, to help remove such differences as existed and to bring out that demonstration of unity which every true lover of the British Empire will appreciate.
I had no intention of referring to my own part in the conference, but hon. gentlemen have made it necessary for me to state my position more fully than I otherwise should have done. I need not detain the House longer, but in conclusion I would again appeal to my hon. friend to consider the wisdom, after the close of this debate, of withdrawing the amendment he 'has submitted.
The amendment is unnecessary and misleading. The position has been made abundantly clear to parliament that the report of the Imperial conference in no way commits this country or this House to anything, nor does it deprive this parliament of any right or power now exercised. To agree to an amendment such as the one now proposed is to create an entirely misleading impression with respect to the contents of the report of the conference, and the significance thereof. Let me take the first clause:
That it is not desirable that this House should be deemed tacitly to have acquiesced in the declarations and recommendations contained in the report of the proceedings of the Imperial conference, 1926.
Suppose that clause is accepted; what is the implication? The implication is that where a resolution of this nature has not been adopted . with reference to previous imperial conferences this House has tacitly acquiesced in the reports of those conferences. For my part I am not prepared to admit that this country is bound by a single report of any imperial conference. As I stated emphatically at the outset, the imperial conference is not a parliament, nor is it a council empowered to lay down policies. It is no more than a gathering of representatives of different parts of the empire delegated to state their views and to indicate their conclusions. I submit, with respect to this report and every other report of any imperial conference, that, except to such extent as this parliament desires to endorse and to be bound by what appears in any of these reports, they have no binding effect whatever. The purpose of the conference is to help as far as possible to bring about some Symmetry on the part of the various parts of the empire in the working out of many problems they have

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
in common; to provide between them some more effective means of cooperation; to lay down broad principles and methods for dealing with such matters as call for joint or common consideration; and to ensure effective cooperation whenever the necessity for cooperation may arise and the parliament concerned may decide upon it. I repeat that imperial conferences are not parliaments or councils empowered to make constitutions for the empire.
I ask the House therefore not to agree to any amendment which will leave the implication that, where there has been no formal resolution with respect to reports of this nature, this House has tacitly acquiesced therein.

speechtext:
The Prime
Minister did not say that. The second paragraph of the amendment reads:
That in the opinion of this House the proceedings of the recent Imperial conference and the declarations and recommendations contained in the report of the Imperial Conference Committee on Inter-imperial Relations should not be binding upon the parliament of Canada until approved by a formal resolution of this House.
All this has already been made perfectly clear; no one in this House has any misconception as to the extent to which the report is binding. There is therefore no need for the House to divide on that point. But take the rest of the clause:
And that until such approval is obtained this government shall not be deemed to be authorized to take any steps to carry into effect the recommendations contained in said report.
This morning the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) complained that sufficient time had not been given to the consideration of trade, of migration and of defence. He thought there had been too much purely academic discussion on the question of status. May I say to my hon. friend that while he paid the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and myself the compliment of being academic and the still greater compliment of apparently having directed the affairs of the conference, we w*ere not responsible for the agenda. We took it as it was presented to us and as it appeared when we got there, and if these constitutional questions assumed
large proportions it was not because of our representations. It must be remembered that the conference was representative of all parts of the British Empire, and that many of these questions were of great concern not only to some of the other governments of the selfgoverning dominions but to the British government as well.
If this amendment is adopted the government is prevented without the approval of parliament from even carrying out the administrative measures mentioned in the report, and may I say that in a very large part what is there in the way of recommendation relates to matters of administration which it is hoped will help bring about a more effective coordination and cooperation. Consider the matter of trade statistics; certain standards are laid down to which it is hoped all parts of the empire will conform. We are to be prevented from even attempting to conform to these standards, while other parts of the empire are prepared to do so. The report suggests certain investigations should be made with respect to certain commodities effecting empire trade but until this parliament formally agrees to it we are supposed to say, "No; we are sorry, but we cannot give our consent to any inquiry being made until parliament formally approves of our so doing". I am sure that on reflection my hon. friend will not wish to press matters that far. Then in the concluding paragraph it is stated:
That it is also the opinion of this House that no amendments should be procured to the British North America Act to give effect to said report or otherwise, which would affect the rights, powers or privileges of all or any of the provinces of Canada, as they now exist under the terms of said act, unless the same are first approved by the legislature of each of the provinces of Canada.
It has been stated over and over again that the position so far as the British North America Act is concerned is now exactly the same as before the conference was held, and there is no need of discussing that act on an amendment bearing upon the report of this conference. The conference was held in October and November of last year, and today the British North America Act is in exactly the same position it was in last September; it stands in exactly the same position, so far as the people of Canada, are concerned as it stood before the conference. What then is the need of bringing the British North America Act into a discussion of the rep or' of this conference?
1916	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
I take a further exception. The amendment goes far beyond the report in its reference to amendments. It says:
-no amendments should be procured to the British North America Act to give effect to the said report or otherwise-
Note the "or otherwise." I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the subject of amendments to the British North America Act is big enough to be dealt with alone and should be discussed in this parliament by itself without being confused with this particular report.
In conclusion may I say that if hon. members will reflect they will, I believe, have reason to feel that in every part of the British Empire to-day there is cause for congratulation that those who happened for the time'being to be in certain representative positions were in agreement on great, broad principles which, understood between them, help to make for more effective unity and greater cooperation between all its parts. I say there is cause for congratulation and I believe the people in all parts of the British Empire are proud and pleased that that position has been reached. Now I ask this House not to destroy the good effect of that work of unity and goodwill performed in London by beginning here in Canada a division with respect to this great question of inter-imperial relations which is so far reaching in its effects on all parts of the empire and as well on imperial relations with other parts of the world.

This amendment does not in any way transgress the subject matter of the Imperial conference; it expresses neither assent nor dissent with regard to a single matter which was discussed at the Imperial conference; it merely affirms principles to which every hon. member of this House will, I believe, readily agree. The first principle is that tacit acquiescence should never bind this [DOT] parliament. But, my hon. friend says, that may have an effect on other conferences. It has had effect already. We bound ourselves by tacit acquiescence in regard to the question of treaty making from 1904 until the end of the war, when we signed the Treaty of Peace. We have never ratified a conference report in that -respect, but by acquiescence we have attained the right to negotiate treaties. I do not think tacit acquiescence should bind us in these matters, and I think the House will agree with me. To the second declaration my hon. friend has already subscribed under ordinary circumstances, and he was ready to move it in this House on December 13, last. It declares that nothing in this retport should bind this parliament until parliament has approved of it. The third principle is that we should not in any way commit ourselves to any legislation or any proposal which in fact or by implication would give us the -power to amend our constitution in any way without the consent of the provinces of Canada.
I submit that these are principles to which we can all subscribe, and if unanimity is desired in this connection-to which I have nc objection-let the Prime Minister accept the amendment. He announced in this House that he would not treat it as a motion of want of confidence, and we do not ask him to do so; we can pass this amendment unanimously and by so doing we will lay down principles with which I am satisfied we all agree in our hearts.
I believe the amendment is right in principle, that it will be found to be right in practice and will be adopted in this country sooner or later, so why divide over it now? Let me also -point out that we do not raise in this amendment a single issue which was raised at the conference; no one can misconstrue this amendment, and for the satisfaction of my right hon. friend I am going to tell hi-m that the amendment was prepared on Saturday morning, and was not thought of until he startled this House on Thursday with the

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext:
The bill is intended to meet in some measure the suggestion contained in the Duncan report which we have been discussing here, and upon which legislation has been introduced with respect to freight rates and other matters of importance to the maritime provinces. It is not, however, confined entirely to the maritime provinces. The assistance proposed to be given under the bill is for the purpose of encouraging the erection of plants for the manufacture of by-product coke. I propose when the House goes into committee to introduce two amendments that will make it very clear that this aid is only to be extended to domestic coke, and will not in any way touch the metallurgical production of coke. The main object of the bill is to encourage the use of Canadian coal in the manufacture of coke, which we hope will in a large way supplant the use of anthracite in the acute fuel areas of central Canada. There has been a great deal of discussion in the House with respect to the fuel situation in what we call "the acute fuel area of Canada," which comprises the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. Although there is a low grade coal available quite close to the boundary of Manitoba, yet that province imports a very considerable quantity of American bituminous and anthracite coals for domestic purposes, as do the other provinces named. This assistance is granted in the hope that it will encourage to some extent the use of

Bonus to Coking Plants
Canadian bituminous coal in the municipalities of Quebec, Montreal and Ottawa, and that the market for this coal will be extended farther provided transportation rates warrant it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext: There is no intention to interfere with the drawback which has always prevailed in connection with the metallurgical production of coke. We are merely putting the domestic coke on a parity with the metallurgical coke on which a drawback is at present given. In addition it is hoped to encourage the consumption of Alberta coal for coking purposes in the city of Winnipeg.

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext:
Will
coking plants at present in existence get the benefit of the proposed subsidy?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext:
No, they
will not. The only way you could benefit plants already in existence would be by granting a bounty. This aid is to encourage the erection of plants for the manufacture of domestic fuel. It is not in any sense a bounty that would be applicable to plants already in existence.
The bill speaks pretty largely for itself and requires little explanation except as to the amounts that it provides for assistance in various localities. The hope is that it will encourage the manufacture of the Canadian product as far west as this city in the eastern part of Canada, and as far east as Winnipeg in the western section of Canada.
A word about the existing plant. There is only one, and it is in the city of Hamilton. This will not in any way interfere with the coke that is manufactured there and distributed throughout the area which that particular plant serves. This assistance is being given for the purpose of supplanting so far as that is possible the use of American coal by coke manufactured from our own bituminous coal. At the present moment the American product is coming into the cities of Montreal and Quebec, and it is necessary to make the assistance fairly substantial owing to the fact, which perhaps our maritime friends will not admit, that there is a considerable difference between the American product and the Nova Scotia product used in the manufacture of coke; not in the coke product itself, but as hon. gentlemen know, the by-product obtained in the manufacture
of coke is of considerable importance and cuts down the manufacturing costs very considerably. The high sulphur content in the Nova Scotia coal makes it difficult to wash the gas, and the sale of the gas, of course, has a tendency to cut down the production costs. That difficulty in connection with washing the gas is not so prevalent in the American product as it is in the Canadian product. I think, however, and the work done by our geological research officers tends to confirm this, although drilling would be necessary to prove it, that there are seams in Nova. Scotia which if opened up would be quite equal to the American product, but at the present moment they are not accessible.
May I say that the agitation carried on for the consumption of Canadian coal has brought the Nova Scotia bituminous coal into this market at Ottawa, so something has been accomplished in that direction. So far as this bill is concerned, it is designed for the purpose of supplanting to a greater degree than at present the importation of American anthracite coal. We have demonstrated that the manufacture of coke from the American product has reduced the tonnage of American [DOT] anthracite coming into Canada from 5,000,000 tons in 1923 to 3,500,000 tons last year, and if rates are so adjusted as to bring Alberta lignite coal into western Ontario, the importations of American anthracite will be reduced by just that much more. We are bending all our energies in that direction with a view to supplanting the importation of American anthracite into this central portion of Canada, and we are asking that this assistance be given for the encouragement of new plants for the manufacture of coke for the purpose of further reducing the anthracite supplies required in eastern Canada.

I want to

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext:
The problem is as to the amount which can be used. I propose to touch briefly on that, and I trust I can disabuse the minister's mind as to the value of the proposals. The development in Winnipeg is so absolutely limited that it will amount to nothing. I think that statement is absolutely true. Apart from this measure a similar bill was placed on the order paper some two or three years ago 'by the present minister. That bill met with such disapproval from the ranks of the hon. minister's own party, that, apart from the attitude of the opposition, the bill was withdrawn and not introduced again. The pressure was too strong, but now, under the excuse of the Duncan commission report, they introduce this vicious measure. The Liberal party appealed to the electorate on the basis of low tariff and anti-special privilege and anti-bonus proposition. Now they propose to introduce as vicious a piece of legislation as ever could emanate from the Tory party. No wonder the leader of the Tory party wishes to rush it through. It is in accordance with their principles. It is one of the most alarming and one of the most repellent features of the whole session. It is not only in this matter that they are deviating from their avowed principles; we have had other instances of special privileges and the giving of rights that were extraordinary, in view of the declarations of my hon. friends opposite. We find the Georgian Bay Canal bill being pushed forward. We find the twenty per cent eastern railway rate reduction put through last night in violation of their own ideals, and probably we will have the Russell patent bill, vicious as it is in its principle; and it will be supported by hon. members opposite. Now we have this legislation. I throw up my hands in despair when we find the great old Liberal party sinking into the morass of Tory legislation. This is the most disgusting and appalling feature of the legislation of this session.
As to the general principles of the bill, there is no question that there is an acute fuel area in the central provinces. There is no question that there is an abundant supply of coal in eastern and western Canada to supply the eastern and western provinces. The one great difficulty is the distance of the supply from the market, and instead of attempting to adjust transportation rates through the railway commission, and instead of taking some action to bring into effect the findings of the Board of Railway Commissioners when made, we find the government trying to meet it by introducing legislation of a character tremendously important and overwhelmingly burdensome. I

Bonus to Coking Plants
am astounded at the action of the Liberal administration. The total anthracite shipped into the country is now 5,000,000 tons. The total coke shipped into the country is 668,121 tons. These figures remain relatively about the same one year with another. At page 8 of the publication of the Dominion Fuel Board, entitled, Coke as a Household Fuel in Central Canada, one can find a complete summary dealing with the exports from United States to Canada of coke and anthracite. As to coke being a substitute for and replacing anthracite, there is no quarrel. He says, and I agree,-and that is the apparent idea in this bill-" we are going to replace by this bill a part of the present importations of anthracite by about 2,000,000 tons now being used in the provinces." I find in this same report, which supports the idea of a subsidy for the coking plant, at page 11, a declaration that anthracite prices are bound to become prohibitive. The reason given is the limited supply in the United States, the growing disinclination of the people of the United States to allow exportation of anthracite to Canada, and in addition to that the steady replacement, which would be enormously increased by satisfactory freight rates, of the anthracite by our own domestic coal. But the conclusion the Fuel board arrived at in connection with this was that the ultimate prices of anthracite in Canada will grow to a point where the people will not be willing to use it. It will be too high, and the people will turn their attention to cheaper fuel. The solution of the problem, rather than establishing a bonus or setting up a subsidized industry, is the adjustment of the freight rates. On that point I will quote from a statement of the Fuel board which corroborates that position. I am not quarrelling with the quality of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick coal. It is true that sometimes sulphur contents are too high to make it possible that the first grade quality coke can be produced from it alone.

The best proof that we can make satisfactory coke out of Nova
Scotia coal is that we have been doing so for a number of years. One hundred per cent would be much better but we feel that 70 per cent use of Nova Scotia coal is a step in the right direction.

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF DOMESTIC FUEL FROM COAL MINED IN CANADA
speechtext:
If that can be shown to the House, it would have been much more patriotic, to use a phrase that has been used so much this afternoon, if the government, if it is sincerely behind the bill had, in introducing it, implied by the very nature of it the use of 100 per cent Canadian coal instead of paying subsidies to plants that will use only seventy per cent Canadian coal. At page 14 of the same publication will be found this statement:
In other words, if coke produced from these coals can be sold at a price which will give heat units equivalent to other fuels, it will rapidly come into favour.
There is no question about that. But note the hypothesis:
If coke produced from these coals can be sold at a price-
The question that is worrying me is whether under this scheme we can produce coke so cheaply and economically that people will buy it instead of the anthracite and other coals that are coming in. A couple of years ago I had the pleasure of visiting the city of Troy, New T ork, and of going over the extensive coking plant they have in that city. I was informed that it was the last word in coke oven plants. I found that that plant was producing 365,000 tons of coke a year, or roughly 1,000 tons a day, but in the production of that the company also produces, as a part of its process, 16,000,000 cubic feet of gas a day. Every authority on coke and on the marketing of coke admits that coke can be satisfactorily and economically marketed only when there is a full and satisfactory market for the gas by-product, which is the principal by-product of the carbonization of coal. In this particular instance in Troy there was a ready market at its door; but I would ask hon. gentlemen to note this and to ask themselves in turn: Is there a single district outside of Montreal and Toronto where similar conditions can be said to exist in Canada? This plant under contract was supplying with gas from its plant no less than the cities of Albany, Troy, Schenectady, Cohoes, Rensslaer, and Watervliet, all of them industrial towns in the Hudson valley. If you can dhow me any single centre in Canada where little industrial cities or towns are grouped closely enough together to make it possible economically and profitably to dispose of the gas by-product, I
Bonus to Coking Plants

admit there would be some sense in establishing or in assisting in the establishment of coking plants. There is no such situation in Canada excepting, as I said before, the two cities of Montreal and Toronto.
There is another point which occurs to me. If a ready market can be found for the gas and if the coke itself will find a ready market at an economic price, then I submit that there is no necessity for a subsidy. The thing should stand on its own feet if it is a commercial proposition. Why is it necessary to undertake to bonus, to subsidize to the extent of four per cent per annum of the total capital cost of the plant in the case of a municipally owned plant and four per cent in the case of a privately-owned plant, if the thing is economically feasible? If it is not economically feasible, why under heaven launch the country into an undertaking that, under pressure, political and otherwise, may develop in Canada another great subsidized industry sapping the taxpayers in annual payments? That is wrong, and I will go further in a few moments in indicating what the actual cost wilt probably be if advantage is taken of this measure.
In the United States I find there are several coking plants already established. There is no question as to the economic feasibility of the carbonization of coal provided that a ready market for the gas by-product is found. There are at least five or six plants, in some cases municipally-owned, in other cases privately-owned, where coking has been going on for some time, and in Great Britain and Germany they not only are experimenting but actually have developed quite a number of plants for the carbonization of coal. This same publication, dealing with this point of markets, states at page 21:
There is a market in Canada for all the coke for domestic fuel that the country can produce, both by coke oven and retort.
There is no question about that. There is in my opinion no superior fuel, not even anthracite, to coke if it is a good coke. I will admit that there is a ready market for the coke itself, but the point is, as I said a moment ago, that unless you can dispose of the principal by-product and the other byproducts, the thing is not commercially profitable, and therefore the development of coking plants is not advisable. The report of the Fuel board itself admits that, unless the market for the by-product can be ascertained, it is not feasible. At page 21 the report states:
Coke ovens cannot be established in every city in central Canada, and can be economically operated selling coke and gas at fair prices- only where there is a market for the gas.

The report of the Fuel board is very specific and dear on that. We pass on then to a survey of the possibilities in this country, and we find that the board actually undertook a survey of the whole market for gas and coke. They chose several cities which I will name in a moment, but they make this com'' ment at page 29:
The cities chosen are those where the domestic gas demand is sufficient to warrant installation of ovens and successfully support a by-product coke plant.
But even then the demand would be only half supplied, because under the contention of the board itself, they can dispose of only a fractional part of the total domestic fuel requirements. The only portion which they cou'd dispose of would be the portion dependent upon the market for the gas byproduct. The cities and districts in which that survey took place were Montreal, Quebec, Ottawa, Toronto, Port Coilborne, Hamilton, London and the border cities. If the total potential market that can be developed for each city and zone is estimated, it would mean a production of roughly in the case of the different towns:
Tons a day

This is not for city requirements alone; this embraces a whole zone.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill was before the select standing com-jnittee on banking and commerce I opposed it; I have * not since had occasion t'o change my mind, but in fact am more opposed to it now than when it was before that committee. Before the bill is passed I think it would be well for this House to consider it carefully, especially in view of the growing importance of insurance in our economic life. After the usual camouflage, this bill provides that this company may increase its capital stock from $1,500,000 to {4,000,000, and that is one of the main purposes of the bill. This increase in the capital stock will be brought about by means of distributing stock bonuses and not by paid up cash at all, and having done this the company will be able to conceal from the participating policyholders and the policyholders in general the actual profits paid on the capital stock, which is the other main purpose of the bill.
We do not want to be unfair to insurance companies; we realize that they have certain responsibilities and that their stocks are more or less speculative, but in view of the fact that the company has already built up a reserve of $56,000,000 from profits, which fund now is the property of the shareholders, I feel that those shareholders have nothing to worry about.

I would like to place on Hansard a short statement concerning this company. The original paid up capital was $305,000 and in premiums another $120,000, or a total of $425,000 actually paid in cash. In 1921 a special dividend of $350,000 was paid1 to the shareholders and stock bonuses to the extent of $845,000 have also been issued, making a total of $1,195,000. Adding this to the amount originally paid in, we have the capital of the company amounting to $1,600,000. The nominal dividend is 15 per cent on this amount, and last year profits of $225,000 were divided among the shareholders on the original investment of $305,000, or at the rate of 73.8 per cent'. On the total paid in capital, including the $120,000 collected in premiums, the fate was 52.9 per cent. If this bill passes the capital stock will be increased to $4,000,000 by distributing bonuses, and with the usual 15 per cent dividend they will divide $600,000 annually among the shareholders which is equal to 141 per cent of the total cash paid in by the shareholders. At present the company does not need to draw on the profits of the participating policyholders in order to pay the 15 per cent on the $1,500,000 of capital, but to show that they intend to do so if this bill passes and they are allowed to increase their capital, they have provided in the bill itself a fixed rate ranging from 3 per cent to 4 per cent which may be taken from the policyholders, so that there can be no question as to their real purpose, and I do not think this is fair to the policyholders. When the president of tlie company appeared before the banking and commerce committee he said that the policyholders were in agreement with the shareholders in this move and that they had approved of the action of the company at the annual meeting. I doubted that statement very much, so as a member of the com-piitl'ee I asked how many policyholders were present at the annual meeting and I think he said there were fifty. I question very much whether there was one of those policyholders who did not have some interest other than that of an ordinary policyholder, but even granting that fifty policyholders were present out of 500,000, that means only one out of every 10,000 was present at the meeting. No formal notice of the meeting was sent to the policyholders, though the president said that some sentence on the company's receipt form advised policyholders of the meeting. I am satisfied that perhaps almost 100 per cent of the policyholders who have no other interest in the company would be opposed to this bill, because it means that the company will be enabled to take money out of their pockets to swell the dividends of the shareholders.

Sun Life Assurance Company
I do not want to ask the House to take my word for it, so I have here some of the evidence given by the former president of this company before the Royal Commission on Life Insurance in 1906. The extracts which I am about to read are found at page 2802 of the evidence taken before that commission, where in reply to a question about the capital, he said:
I have been repeatedly requested to allow shareholders to pay up more and I have always refused. . . . Simply because we did not need the money.
The examiner made the following statement:
That is an excellent reason. You did not need the money, and there was no reason why you should permit shareholders to put in more money to be drawing down interest.
His reply was as follows:
Taking away more of the profits belonging to the policyholders. Of course I fully appreciate that I am under oath and you want all the information that I have. The reason that guided me particularly in refusing was always that it would be a tax on the policyholders.
Now I have a great deal of respect for the Superintendent of Insurance for the Dominion, Mr. Finlayson. I think he is one of the very few men who will not be swayed by any influence other than his own good judgment.
I know that he is opposed to this bill and rightly so. It is unfair to the policyholders; it is almost a breach of contract with the policyholders. In the second place when the camouflage is removed it is nothing more or less than an attempt to conceal the actual profits being paid to the shareholders. I pointed out	that	they will	be enabled topay $600,000	annually,	or at	the rate of 141per cent, if	this	bill	goes	through. Thisprinciple has	been	put	in force by so many
companies and corporations in Canada that its effect is like that of the tariff-it is bearing too heavily upon the public. I think if there is anything this parliament can do to stop this practice it should be done, and I for one intend to vote against this bill on its third reading.

subtopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I apposed this bill in
committee; I am glad of the opportunity of opposing it again to-night. When the bill passed committee I do not think one-third of the membership was present owing to the fact that there were other committees sitting simultaneously. I am of the opinion that if we had had a fairly good representation in the committee the bill would not have passed. It passed by a very small margin as it was.
I wish to oppose this bill chiefly because I regard it as a device by means of which 3264S-122
the shareholders of the Sun Life Assurance Company will be permitted to collect a larger toll from the profits of the policyholders. This is not the first device which the company has practised in this regard. I wish to substantiate that statement by quoting briefly from the report of the Royal Commission on fjife Insurance, dated February 28, 1906. I quote from page 20 of that report:
During 1891, and the first half of 1892, dividends at the rate of twelve per cent, and since and including the latter half of 1892, at fifteen per cent, have been declared, besides the bonus of 2J per cent upon the old stock in 1897.
Carrying to the credit of the shareholders' account the ascertained proportion of profits and interests has not, however, enabled the company to pay these dividends, and from time to time the directors have resorted to various devices for the purpose of increasing the shareholders' account, so as to enable it to pay the dividends which have been paid.
The first of these devices was to credit the practically defunct accident branch with considerable sums of money, upon the theory that that branch in years past had been charged more than its proportion of the general expenses of the company. The accident branch being so credited out of the current profits, the sums so credited were brought into the shareholders' account, for the purpose of augmenting it and so enabling the dividends to be paid. Three sums were so credited to the accident branch and brought in to the detriment of the policyholders; $2,000 in 1895; $4,000 in 1900; and $30,000 in 1902; and the evidence is that there are still at the credit of the accident branch considerable sums of money, the intention being to bring these also into the shareholders' account. It is manifest that in revising the charges made in past years to the accident branch, the directors of the present day have undertaken to overrule what may be presumed to have been the well informed and deliberate decision of the directors of former years as to the proper proportion of expenses to be charged to that branch, and your commissioners think it clear that the revision was undertaken solely as a device for maintaining the shareholders' account.
Another improper means by which the shareholders' account has been enabled' to provide the dividends paid to shareholders is by similarly revising the rate of interest allowed upon capital in addition to its share of the profits in past years. The method adopted has been to go through the years as far back as 1877 and to allow, instead of the rates -which were allowed, a rate of six per cent, which has been imposed at six per cent, compound interest, from 1877 down. The result of this has been to bring into the shareholders' account $9,088.34 (in 1901).
A third method of swelling the shareholders' account has been to go back to the year 1897, when the new capital was issued at a premium of $30 per share, and to bring into the general shareholders' account interest, compounded at six per cent, upon that premium. This revision of the earlier dealing with this premium, to the prejudice of policy holders, was also, in the opinion of your commissioners, improper. In this way the shareholders' account was swollen in 1905 by the sum of $37,930.73.

Sun Lije Assurance Company

I think that extract, Mr. Chairman, will be sufficient to show that the company is not beyond practising devices for the purpose of increasing the profits of the shareholders.
Now I want to have a look at section 1 for a minute. Section 1 provides that at the end' of the present year the percentage of participating policyholders' profits taken by the shareholders shall be reduced to four per cent. This is fixing the rate to be received by statute, and by so fixing the rate the shareholders are deprived of the privilege of reducing the percentage of their profits even if they should desire to do so. Subsequently it is provided that there shall be reductions to 3| per cent and 3 per cent. First, I protest against the fixing of these profits by statute. But the most objectionable phase of the first section of the bill is that it represents the company as being magnanimous. It will sound good to be able to say that they are only being paid four per cent. But when we take this section into consideration with sections 2 and 3 we will find that the company is not as magnanimous as would appear under section 1. I shall have occasion in a few minutes to refer to the meaning of this as brought out in sections 2 and 3. Meanwhile I would point out that section 1 of the bill represents a curtailment of the power of the shareholders to reduce the percentage of profits by a majority vote. It appears to do something in favour of the policyholders, while really it is strengthening the position of the shareholders at the expense of the former. It is very doubtful if any considerable percentage of the policyholders of this company know anything at all about this bill, and it is to be doubted if any percentage of those that do know understand its real significance; for unless one clause were explained in relation to the other it would be very difficult for an ordinary layman, unless he was looking for it in particular, to know just exactly what is the real meaning of the bill.
Now I want to deal with the second section of the bill, and I ask, why this company should desire to increase its capital? The reason why any company would want to increase its capital would be, I suppose, one of two. It might want to increase its capital in order to make the company more stable. For instance, if there is too narrow a margin between the assets and liabilities of the company it might be advisable to increase the capital. I do not think, however, that the Sun Life Assurance Company iof Canada would like the people of this country to be-
TMr. Irvine.]
lieve that the reason why they are asking for this increase in capital is in order to stabilize the company because of there being too narrow a margin between assets and liabilities. Indeed, there is no such danger.
There is another reason why a company might wish to increase its capital, and that is in order to draw greater profits. If this company is in need of more capital to guarantee the stability of the company, then perhaps it would be the duty of parliament to pass this bill; but if, on the other hand, the company is in good financial standing and further capital is not required for good business reasons, then an extra two million dollar capital would simply be an extra burden on the company, and the profits paid thereon would not have been honestly earned. Moreover, all such profits must eventually be gathered from the policyholders. If this latter be the position obviously parliament would be doing a very .great wrong in passing this bill.
I propose to inquire into the position of the company in this regard: Does the Sun Life require an additional two million capital? Before referring specifically to the financial position of the company and to the shareholders, I wish to make an observation or two in a general way in respect to capital in relation to the insurance business, and then to refer specifically to the paid up capital of this company.
There is a very great doubt, Mr. Chairman, whether capital is required at all in insurance companies. We will all agree that in most business enterprises capital is essential, and we might even go so far as to say that in the initial stages of an insurance company a certain amount of capital is essential. But when the insurance company has become established, then the more capital it has, the more dangerous it is for the company, for that capital is unnecessary; it becomes an additional burden upon the company. Writing insurance is the best insurance for an insurance company. If the stability of any established insurance company in Canada were to depend upon the amount of capital subscribed, there is not one of them that is safe; but that is not the basis of their stability. The basis of their stability is their policyholders and the business that they do. The insurance business is the safest business in the world, and capital is the greatest hindrance that it has. If we are going to permit this company after it has been established for so many years to increase its capital now that it has become so prosperous that it does not know what to do with its

Sun Lije Assurance Company
profits, I think we should be very remiss in our duty indeed. All that one has to do is to imagine that the amount of profits now being paid on the capital stock of insurance companies were left to swell the reserves; we can readily see how much better the position would be in that case. But if you increase that capital, an extra charge for profits will be made directly on the policyholders, and to that extent you would embarrass the company.
That capital is not required in well-established insurance companies may be proved by (he tendency to-day towards mutualization. Some of the greatest insurance companies in the world have become entirely mutual. For instance, we have the Prudential Insurance Company mutualized. Then we have that company which is I believe the greatest of its kind in the world, the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, with its Canadian head office in this city; that company, I believe, is entirely mutual. I understand that the stockholders were bought out for one-third the value of the stock at the time the Change was made. The company is now a mutual one, and its shareholders are its policyholders. Not one cent of profit is taken from the earnings of the company to pay stockholders.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say that it would be more in keeping with the modem tendency if the Sun Life Assurance management were taking steps towards mutualizing the company and doing away with all stock whatsoever, rather than trying to increase its capital, which would mean the gathering of more profits from the policyholders.
Again, the policyholders do not need additional capital for their security. On the contrary, it is a detriment to the policyholders, because it will involve paying a larger amount of the participating policyholders' profits to the shareholders than would otherwise be necessary to provide reasonable dividends. If we authorize the increased capital asked for in this bill, it will no doubt be distributed in the way of stock bonuses or special dividends to which the participating policyholders will be called upon to subscribe.
The present paid up capital of the Sun Life Assurance Company is $1,500,000. Let us stop to realize that no other insurance company in Canada has such a large subscribed capital. Indeed, no other company has a capital exceeding $1,000,000, and yet we have one of the greatest, perhaps the greatest Canadian company not satisfied with that amount of capital but coming here and asking us to increase it. Of that present paid up
32649-12Zi
capital of $1,500,000, $1,195,000 has been paid by way of stock bonuses or special dividends, and only $305,000 has been paid in cash by the shareholders. I want you to take notice of this, Mr. Chairman. The annual amount required to pay the dividend is now $225,000, so the shareholders of the Sun Life Assurance Company collect 73 per cent annually on their investment, that is 73 per cent on the amount' of money that they actually put into this company. If the capital of the company is increased to $4,000,000, as is asked for in this bill, and is distributed by way of stock bonuses or special dividends, as will almost certainly be done, and if the present rate of dividend of 15 per cent is continued, the amount annually required for shareholders' dividends will be $600,000. The amount of capital actually paid in to the company in cash by the shareholders would remain as at present, $305,000, and the annual dividends therefore would represent 197 per cent profit per annum on the capital originally invested in the company. Surely a condition of that sort is worthy of the attention of this committee. Surely when these facts are placed before us we shall realize our responsibility to the policyholders, who may be regarded as the general public. These profits can only be paid at the expense of the policyholders. The profit which now goes to shareholders on unnecessary capital should either increase the profits of policyholders or go to the reduction of the cost of insurance. Policyholders' funds are virtually trust funds. In this regard I wish to make another short quotation from the report of the commission already referred to, under the heading, " The relation of directors to policyholders and their interests, including questions of individual or concentrated control, and the powers and duties of directors with regard to investments and management generally":
It seems to the commission of importance to define the nature and position of the funds resulting from the operation of insurance companies. Save in so far as capital stock plays a part, these funds are either a reserve kept in hand to discharge the insurance obligation or a surplus resulting from a charge upon the persons insured in excess of what it has cost to insure their lives. The policyholder contributes both reserve and surplus, and where business is done upon the participating plan it is the surplus moneys that are called profits.

And what is the character of these funds? Are the purposes to which they are being devoted consistent with that character? When the House rose at six o'clock I was drawing attention to the report of the Dominion Fuel Board entitled, Coke as a Household Fuel in Central Canada, Bulletin No. 5, from which I quote:
Although there is room for a plant in all the cities mentioned, the first plants built will have the advantage of picking the cream of the market.

I come now to the other by-products. The possibility of a gas market for these coking plants is discussed in this report, but to my amazement it occupies only two pages, and there is no indication whatever-either by survey, inspection, by tabulation of statistics, or by a compilation of any figures-as to the potential markets for gas. There is no indication whatever in it that there will be a market available for the gas to be produced from these plants.
Ammonia sulphate is the next by-product, in point of volume, from the carbonization of coal. At page 44 there is one short page given to discussing the market possibilities in this country, in one sentence of which the limited nature of the market at the present time is indicated by the statement that "an educational campaign, if properly attempted, should create a demand for home consumption." There is no doubt but that there is a market for ammonia sulphate in the West Indies and some other places where they have been using it for some time. Possibly the plant at Montreal could dispose of its surplus in that way; but the other plants at Ottawa, Toronto, or wherever they may be established, would find it very difficult to take advantage of the proposal from an economic standpoint. Of course if a plant were established in Quebec, it could avail itself of the ocean transportation to the West Indies.
The next by-product is light oils. Now the report itself definitely lays down the statement that in plants of 500 tons carbonizing capacity per day, or less, it is not profitable to recover the light oils. The suggestion is made that they should be left in the coke, and to that degree at least add more bulk and more volatile matter to it, but you would be losing a valuable by-product by so doing. I understand that in England and in Germany, since the close of the war many investigations and experiments have been carried on in this line of work their endeavour being to reduce the

minimum quantity of gas produced from coal and increase in proportion the light oils available, which of course would, be very valuable; but unless the plant is capable of producing at least 1,500 gallons per day, the extraction of oil is not profitable. When we take the figures I have quoted this afternoon showing the total production per day per plant in the zones outlined in the report, in only two instances will it be found profitable to put up a plant of this nature and produce and take out the oil as one of the by-products. Tar products, of course, are always valuable and readily disposed of. There would be eight or twelve gallons to every ton.
As to breeze, that product-could be disposed of to industrial steam and other furnaces, or could be disposed of to a limited extent in the plant itself.
Now at .pages 114 and 115 of the report I find estimates given of the cost of plants. I gave the House this afternoon an estimate of my own of the cost of a plant producing a thousand tons of coke per day. That estimate was based on the cost of the Troy plant, one of the most efficient and up-to-date plants in North America to-day, and which was visited by some hion. members opposite as well as the members of the committee a couple of yeais ago. The Troy plant cost about -three and a half millions, but the labour conditions in the plant, and in the district surrounding it, were deplorable. I asked Eon. gentlemen who were there if they were not struck by the pallor, the emaciation, the miserable, wretched physical condition of the workers and their families within the vicinity of both the blast furnaces and the coking plant. I found out on examination-by inviting statements from some of the foremen and others-that the wage paid ordinary labour in the plant was 42-| cents an hour. The highest wage paid in the plant was paid to technical workers, that is expert men like the acetylene welders, or men engaged in work of that mechanical character. They are paid 75 cents an hour. This condition in the United States where conditions are supposed to be so splendid. Forty-two and -one half cents an hour for the average labour; 75 cents an hour for the expert or dangerous labour. I asked:	How
many hours a day do you work? And to my utter amazement I found that these men in the plant were working twelve hours a- day.

Walking out in the city of Troy, Mr. Speaker, it occurred to me to examine the retail prices in order that we would have some idea of what relief we might expect in this country under a similar proposal, and I found right there beside the plant, with no railway charges to pay, nothing but the wagons to haul, a price of $11 a ton. The coal for coking in Troy cost them from $5 to $5.40 per ton. The immediate consumer in the little city, if it was economically feasible to build such a plant, might gain some advantage, say about $1 per ton over the anthracite price.
As to the possibility of developing this trade to any extent outside the city, that is hopeless on account of the present railway rates. I will deal with that point before I close. In the Hamilton plant which was mentioned this afternoon, I find that they are using entirely American coal. They are using that under drawback, and 70 per cent of it is the celebrated Elkhorn coal, which is a very high volatile coal from the United States, and 30 per cent of it is the equally celebrated Pokahontas coal, a bituminous, low volatile coal. They are using 100 per cent American coal in that plant, and I ask you how? By
securing from this Liberal government a drawback of 99 per cent of the cost of the coal that is used for this purpose.
The minister informed me this afternoon, in answer to a question, that it was not the intention of the administration to affect in any way the drawback, and that it was to be continued. At the same time the minister challenged me when I stated that under this bill there would not be one dollar of advantage to the Alberta coal producer, and indeed I am beginning to be a little timid of its effects elsewhere if this drawback is to be continued. Let me point out one or two facts in connection with it. Specific mention has been made of the city of Winnipeg. The minister thought that a plant in Winnipeg would be able to develop a partial market for our Alberta coal. The Winnipeg Electric Company have operated a gas-producing plant for many years. Some time ago they introduced a battery of by-product coke ovens. The primary object of both plants is the same, that is, the production of gas, with coke as a by-product. This by-product plant was built prior to the tariff amendment of 1925 which admitted United States bituminous coal for coke-making purposes practically free of duty. The United States coal used in the gas producing plant is not entitled to a drawback of duty, but coal imported for use in the by-product ovens, although used for the same purpose is entitled to the di-awback or subsidy. Every ton of coke produced in this plant from American coal is sold in direct competition with Alberta domestic coal in Winnipeg. Note that, Mr. Speaker: Every ton of coke produced from American coal in this plant is sold in direct competition with our own Alberta coal.
I do not think I need go further than that simple statement to indicate to the minister that any belief he may have had that this policy would provide a market for our Alberta coal in Winnipeg is dissipated and must remain so as long as that drawback continues. Let me say this. Although I have from time to time deplored the practice of imposing duties, and I do still deplore it, yet I say to the minister that there is nothing so utterly inconsistent and ridiculous as imposing a duty for certain purposes, such as to keep out a commodity which is entering inito competition with our own commodities in this country, and then upon pressure from private interest, for private exploitation and private gain, to permit the importation of that commodity on a drawback duty of 99 per cent. That is a most vicious principle, and I am sure the minister agrees with me.
