My hon. friend has
a most peculiar manner of showing his sympathy. My hon. friend comes as I do from a Canadian province which possesses vast and extensive coal deposits. I know he must be as anxious as I am to see developed in this country a national fuel policy under which Canada will so far as possible be made independent of a foreign nation in the matter of her fuel supply. And in spite of the fact that my hon. friend has used his voice and intimates that he will exercise his vote to prevent this bill from going through, whenever he or any of his colleagues or associates from Alberta brings up in this House any measure dealing with transportation or anything else tending to improve the condition of the coal industry of that province, or to increase its coal output, or to bring that coal to the markets of central Canada, then in direct opposition to the attitude that he has taken to-night, my voice and my much inferior abilities will be raised in support of the legitimate claims of the province from whence he comes.
My hon. friend in the first part of his speech said there were certain objections which could not be met in respect of the establishment of coking plants. One of the chief objections was that we had no allabsorbing market for our gas such as the House of Commons provides on certain occasions. If he will refer to the report from which he quoted at some length to-night, he will find that the author of that report takes an entirely different view. He will find for example that the very eminent engineer who compiled the report from which he quoted stated in it that he made an extensive survey of conditions in Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, and Port Colborne. He then goes on to say:
The cities chosen are those where the domestic gas demand is sufficient to warrant installation of ovens and successfully support a by-product coke plant.
He also states:
Other localities such as the "border" cities, can erect plants as soon as the industrial or domestic gas demand is sufficient.
He goes on further to say on page 34 of the report that at the present time there is a total market in Canada for some 2,628,000 tons of household fuel. The writer, having in mind the possible disposition of the gas and other by-products, points out that by the establishment of coke ovens at the present time, a production of 1,376,300 tons of American anthracite could be displaced by Canadian coke. I think that is sufficient evidence of the feasibility of the project which this bill has in mind to encourage.
I am in favour of this bill because it aims at the further development of the great coal resources of the. Dominion. It is intended to bring about a wider distribution of Canadian coal in Canadian markets. I am in favour of it because it is a step in the direction of a national fuel policy for Canada, and that is something which should meet with the approbation of every patriotic Canadian who has the industrial and commercial interests of Canada at heart. Coal is one of the basic elements in the industrial progress of any nation, for no great industrial achievement is possible unless a nation possesses coal deposits and can properly utilize them. Coal is by far the most important of all the mineral products, and next to coal in importance is iron. The existence of. coal and iron deposits throughout the world has profoundly influenced modern civilization. The greatest commercial nations in the world to-day are the United States, Germany and England all of which owe their industrial and commercial greatness in no small measure to their coal deposits. If Canada is to take its place in the sun industrially and commercially, if it is to occupy that position in industry and commerce which a 'bountiful nature ordained should be ours, then I say this parliament must of necessit3r take steps to inaugurate a national fuel policy. And this is one such step. I may say to my hon. friends that when they bring into parliament any measure calculated to assist *the coal industry of Alberta we from the maritime provinces will support it just as we had expected that they would support us in connection with this bill.
It is an anomalous, an illogical position for Canada to allow the central provinces to depend upon a friendly but none the less rival industrial power for their fuel supply. It is a situation that should not obtain because in Canada we possess 17 per cent of the total coal reserves of the world. Our concern should
Bonus to Coking Plants

be to bring Canadian coal to our industrial centres, and this can be done if proper measures are taken by this parliament.
This bill will not only be of advantage to the province of Nova Scotia, but it will foe of very material advantage to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. At the present time these provinces depend almost entirely upon American anthracite for their domestic needs. That is an insecure position. It is a position which no self-respecting country should care to be in. It is a dangerous position for any province to tolerate. It is dangerous for this reason chiefly, that according to mineralogists the supply of American anthracite coal is being rapidly depleted. Already, as those who have given study to the question know, what were two very important sources of supply of American anthracite, namely, the Carbondale and Scranton districts, which ten years ago were important sources of supply, 'have by this time petered out, and to-day they produce practically no coal. In 1924 there were presented to congress no fewer than three resolutions to the effect that the United States government should place an embargo on the exportation of American anthracite. What would foe the position of central Canada today had such action been taken by the government to the south of us. It is time for us to take serious cognizance of the situation and to see to it that there shall be available some suitable substitute in the event of the supply of American anthracite being at any time cut off. But apart from the uncertainty of being able to secure American anthracite we have the positive assurance that as the years go on, according as the American supply diminishes, the price of anthracite coal to the consumer in Canada will go up. I venture the prediction that within half a decade if the people of Ontario and Quebec can obtain any American anthracite at all, they will have to pay a very much higher price for it than they are paying now. I say, therefore, that this bill the object of which is to displace as far as possible, American anthracite by a fuel which is superior to it, and which can be and is sold a,t a lower price, will materially assist the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It will also greatly assist Nova Scotia inasmuch as the coal industry is one of the most important of our activities. Upon that industry almost one-fifth of our population depend for their livelihood, and the great problem we have to face in our coal industry is our inability to provide employment for our workmen in winter. When our coal -is banked throughout the winter it generally breaks up and consequently it is more difficult to dispose of. Tt is not

so easy to sell it in that state, and the rehandling charges add materially to the cost of the coal. It has therefore become practically impossible for us to bank coal in winter, although this would provide employment in that season. speechtext: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the third reading of Bill No. 225, respecting the Halifax harbour commissioners.

In connection with this bill, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that the situation in connection with Halifax harbour is somewhat different from that of any other port perhaps in the Dominion, inasmuch as the property there, outside of that owned by the railways and other departments of the government, is all private property. The government and railway property, that is, the elevator coming

Halifax Harbour Commission
under Trade and Commerce, and the wharves coming under the Department of Railways, are at the present time very well managed, economically managed, I think I can say. It is these properties, as I understand this bill, that will be taken over by the' commission. Different departments of the government will be paid for these properties by money raised, I suppose, on debentures guaranteed by the government, and the private property will remain as it is. In Montreal I think all the harbour is under the control of the board, and that all the property is owned by the board. Comparing these two bills, the city of St. John is interested to an amount beyond $2,000,000 which will be returned to them by the commission there, and practically the whole of the harbour in St. John will be under the harbour commission. Such is not the case in Halifax. As I understand the proposal, the only transfer of property will be that now owned by the government and managed by the government. The transfer to the harbour commission in Halifax means, that in order to pay the interest on the moneys paid for these properties, to pay the commissioners and to pay the management of the whole organization, goods will be taxed an amount per ton. I do not know how much-which somebody has to pay, whether it is the ships carrying those goods or whether it is the goods themselves-and that tax will have to be paid in order to keep up the harbour commission. At the present time charges such as will be introduced by the harbour commissioners are borne, rightly I think, by the railways. They are included in the through freight rate, and there is no further tax on those goods. That tax on these goods for the upkeep of the harbour and of the commission will be a tax placed upon the traffic of the port to which the port is not now subject, and to that extent it will be a disadvantage to the port as an outlet and an inlet for Canadian trade. I may say that in that connection I received a telegram from Halifax as follows:
Joint committee of city council and board of trade have wired Colonel Ralston approving of the harbour commission bill but wish to only have it put :n force by order in council, giving time for a conference with the government to work out details before any appointment commissioners. Also adding a clause giving commission power to use funds to canvass trade for the port.
The latter suggestion with regard to funds to canvass for trade would be in line I think with the Duncan report, because it suggested that a commission would be able to advertise the port, and possibly through that advertising bring trade there. The request seems to be a fairly reasonable one, and perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) may see his way clear to meet the wishes of our Halifax friends, the board of trade and city council, by adding a clause such as they suggest, and also giving permission, if such is necessary, that the expense in connection with the advertising of the port be borne by the commissioners. Apparently, if the details can be worked out satisfactorily in connection with the change of management down there, there will be no difficulty at all with regard to putting the bill in force. But the request on the part of Halifax seems reasonable, and I hope that the minister may see his way clear to deal with the bill in such a way that the wishes of our Halifax friends can be fully considered. I can assure hon. members that it is a very important matter. In looking over the bill I find that it requires a good deal of study. There is a good deal of detail that should be worked out in connection with the city of Halifax, which is an exceptional port in the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I cannot see any difference between the situation in Halifax and the situation in St. John. I think the argument of my hon. friend is rather an argument against one of the recommendations of the Duncan report, because there is no alternative and there is nothing indefinite in the recommendation of the Duncan report. What they want is the organization of a harbour commission. We are complying exactly with the recommendation of the Duncan report with regard to the incorporation of a harbour commission, and I feel that I cannot accept the suggestion of my hon. friend to add a clause that the bill become law only by proclamation.

Would the minister permit me to make a suggestion which I think will meet the idea of my hon. friend', which he may not have thought of? Section 5 states that the board shall consist of three commissioners to be appointed by the governor in council. The commission does not come into existence until the governor in council appoints it. If the minister would give to my hon. friend, and through him to the board of trade of Halifax, the assurance that the commissioners would not be appointed until there was an opportunity of hearing the board of trade, it would accomplish exactly what my hon. friend suggests.

satisfactory.
